mc-pahani-ror1b: Key Highlights Telangana runs on TWO parallel record systems for every parcel: the Pahani (the village’s annual working diary of the land) and the RoR 1-B (the ownership register). Reading only one is reading half the truth. Both descend from a 150-year lineage — Salar Jung’s reforms → the Land Revenue Act 1317 Fasli (1907) → sethwar, tippan and village map → the 1954-55 khasra pahani → the 1971 RoR Act → 1989 passbooks → Dharani (2020) → the Bhu Bharati Act (2025). Old generations of the record still WIN cases today. The law’s big promise: every entry in the Record of Rights is PRESUMED TRUE until the contrary is proved — a presumption, not a guarantee. The law’s big limit, from the Supreme Court down: revenue entries prove POSSESSION and support claims — they do not by themselves confer, create or extinguish TITLE. Title comes from registered deeds, grants and statutory vesting. Dharani (2020) thinned the record and dropped the enjoyment column; over 18 LAKH acres of patta land landed in the prohibited Part-B list. The Bhu Bharati Act 2025 exists to repair exactly that — restored 11-column Pahani, notices before amendments, a real appeal ladder, and a one-year correction window closing 13 April 2026. This masterclass walks every column, every era, every ruling and every fraud — with an example for each. Budget 25–30 minutes. Worth it: these two documents decide every land deal you will ever do. Part 1 — Why two records exist at all Start with the question nobody asks: why does the government keep TWO separate books about the same field? Because the state historically cared about two different things. It cared about TAX — who must pay land revenue this year, on how much land, growing what, watered how — and that produced the Pahani , an annual working diary of each parcel, refreshed every agricultural year. And it cared about RIGHTS — who holds the parcel, how they got it, what claims sit on it — and that produced the Record of Rights , whose ownership extract is the 1-B . Tax needs freshness; rights need permanence. Two needs, two books. Example: The shop analogy that makes it stick: the Pahani is the shop’s DAILY REGISTER — who opened the shutter today, what stock moved, who was behind the counter. The 1-B is the shop’s OWNERSHIP FILE — the partnership deed, who owns what share, which bank holds a charge. A stranger behind the counter for five years (an entry in the daily register) eventually becomes a legal problem for the ownership file — which is exactly what happens when a tenant sits in the Pahani’s cultivator column for years while the 1-B says someone else owns the land. Hold that model through everything below: Pahani = the land’s life this year. 1-B = the land’s legal identity across years. Every fraud, every court case and every verification trick in this masterclass is some version of the two books disagreeing. Part 2 — The 150-year story (why the old records still matter) Telangana’s records did not begin with a website. Each era left a layer, and — this is the practical point — the OLDER layers outrank the newer ones when a correction case is fought, because they are closer to the original survey. Here is the whole lineage: Era Record created What it is 1870s–1907 Salar Jung’s revenue reforms → Land Revenue Act, 1317 Fasli Hyderabad State’s Diwan orders scientific measurement of all land; the 1907 Act mandates one sethwar and one village map per village, one tippan per survey number Settlement era SETHWAR (the “A” Register) The foundation record: every survey number’s extent, ownership, nature (patta/inam/government), soil class, irrigation source. Changes issue as SUPPLEMENTARY sethwars Settlement era TIPPAN (Field Measurement Book) + VILLAGE MAP The tippan is the measured sketch of each survey field; the village map is the index that lets an officer find any field on the ground — the tools for boundary disputes and encroachment detection 1954-55 KHASRA PAHANI The great post-Nizam field census — the pahani of 1954-55 recorded pattadar, extent and pote kharab parcel by parcel. THE reference record for “what was true at the start” 1955–58 SESALA PAHANI Three years of cultivation records across six crop seasons — crucially, it recorded PROTECTED TENANTS Correlation WASOOL BAQI The bridge register linking OLD survey numbers to NEW ones village by village — how you trace a parcel across renumbering 1971 RoR Act (AP/Telangana Rights in Land & Pattadar Pass Books Act) Modern Record of Rights: village-wise register of owners, pattadars, mortgagees, occupants; SECTION 6: every entry presumed true until contrary proved; periodic RoR exercises (1979-80, 1989-90) 1989 PATTADAR PASSBOOK system The landmark: a physical book in the farmer’s hand combining the record extract with a title document — the direct ancestor of today’s Passbook-cum-Title Deed 2020 RoR Act 2020 + DHARANI portal Registration and mutation fused into one portal — but the record was THINNED, the enjoyment column dropped, and 18+ lakh acres of patta land fell into the prohibited Part-B list 2025 BHU BHARATI (Record of Rights in Land) Act The repair: restored 11-column pahani, Bhudhaar parcel IDs, notice-before-amendment, a four-rung appeal ladder, Land Tribunals, sada bainama regularisation, and the one-year correction window Definition — Fasli year: the agricultural calendar the records run on, inherited from the Mughal revenue system. Convert roughly by adding 590: fasli 1425 ≈ 2015-16, fasli 1435 ≈ 2025-26. When an old pahani says “fasli 1364”, that is 1954-55 — the khasra pahani year. Example: Why the lineage is not trivia: in a correction fight, the side holding the OLDER official paper usually wins. A Rangareddy family disputing a wrong Dharani-era name entry does not argue with screenshots — they produce the khasra pahani of 1954-55 showing the grandfather as pattadar, the sesala pahani showing the family cultivating, and the 1989 passbook. Three generations of state-issued paper against one migration error: the Tahsildar corrects the record. That is why this masterclass teaches the old records too — they are your ammunition, not history. Example: And why the surveys matter: a CAG audit found that of the records the 1907 Act requires, only 4,712 sethwars and 7,392 village maps survived in the audited districts — the rest were MISSING, and no re-survey had been done in 60+ years. Every missing sethwar is a village where “what was originally true” is provable only with difficulty. When the drone resurvey and LPM numbers arrived (previous classes), they were fixing THIS. Part 3 — The Pahani, column by column The Pahani (also called Adangal, formally “Village Account No. 3”) is prepared by village revenue staff and maintained under the Tahsildar, updated every fasli. Dharani cut it to a stub; the Bhu Bharati Act restored the full multi-column format — the famous “11 columns”. Here is every column and what a professional reads in it: Column What it records The pro read Survey number / sub-division (hissa) The parcel’s identity — e.g. 145/A, not just 145 After family partitions, the PARENT number stops working on portals; search the sub-division. A deed citing 145 for land that is really 145/A/2 is sloppy drafting that will bite at registration Khata number The holder’s ACCOUNT — groups all parcels one person holds in the village One khata, many survey numbers: the fastest way to see a seller’s full village holding Pattadar name (+ father’s name) The recorded holder Must match the deed and Aadhaar to the SPELLING. Father’s name is your tiebreaker among namesakes Anubhavadar / enjoyment (sagu) Who ACTUALLY occupies and cultivates THE column Dharani deleted and Bhu Bharati restored. Pattadar ≠ anubhavadar = tenancy or possession dispute until proven otherwise Land nature Patta / Sarkari / Assigned / Inam The ten-second deal filter: Patta = proceed; Sarkari = government, stop; Assigned = welfare land, leave Classification Tari (wet) / Metta (dry) / Garden / Shikam / Waste Sets honest value and legal use. Tari is irrigated and pricier; shikam is tank-bed land — a flooding and title minefield; waste may have no private ownership history at all Water source Canal / tank / borewell / rain-fed Cross-check against the classification: “wet” land with no water source listed is a classification worth challenging Total extent vs cultivable extent + pote kharab The whole parcel vs the usable part Pote kharab is the unusable portion (rocks, paths, nala). A 5-00 acre parcel with 0-20 guntas pote kharab SELLS as 5 acres but FARMS as 4-20 — and conversion authorities treat the two portions differently Soil class / water rate Settlement-era productivity grading Drives old assessment and still surfaces in ceiling calculations (soil classes A–K decide how many acres one family may hold) Crops by season What was grown each kharif/rabi, on how much The cultivation PROOF: 54B tax claims, crop loans and PMFBY insurance all lean on these entries. Empty crop columns on “farmland” = a record that will not support an agricultural-income story Liabilities / encumbrances Loans, charges, attachments recorded at revenue level Reads ALONGSIDE the EC — an MRO-level charge here may never appear in any EC search Definition — Guntas: the unit under the acre: 1 acre = 40 guntas; 1 gunta = 121 square yards. A holding written “3-25” means 3 acres 25 guntas = 3.625 acres. Learn to read the dash — half the extent mismatches amateurs “find” are just misread guntas. Example: Worked read #1 — the clean parcel: Survey 88/2, khata 214, pattadar K. Narsimha s/o Ramulu, anubhavadar K. Narsimha (same man), nature Patta, classification Metta (dry), source borewell, extent 2-00 / cultivable 1-38 (2 guntas pote kharab for a farm path), crops: cotton kharif fasli 1434, chillies rabi. Every column agrees with the story the seller told you. This is what boring — and buyable — looks like. Example: Worked read #2 — the same parcel, poisoned: identical row, except anubhavadar reads “B. Yellaiah” and the crop columns show Yellaiah’s paddy for six consecutive faslis. Narsimha still owns it — but Yellaiah has six years of state-recorded cultivation, the raw material of a tenancy/possession claim (remember the sesala pahani’s protected tenants: under Section 38-E of the Tenancy Act 1950, long-recorded cultivators could be DEEMED OWNERS). Same owner, same land — the enjoyment column just moved this deal from “negotiate price” to “resolve occupant first, in writing, or walk”. Example: Worked read #3 — the pote kharab surprise: a 10-00 acre “venture-ready” parcel shows cultivable 8-10. Where did 1-30 go? The column says nala (stream) + rocky outcrop. For a plotting developer that is not a footnote — the nala brings buffer-zone rules and layout dead space. The Pahani told you the site plan before the surveyor did. Part 4 — The RoR 1-B, and the presumption that powers it The 1-B is the ownership extract of the Record of Rights: pattadar, father’s name, khata, survey numbers, extent, MODE OF ACQUISITION (purchase / inheritance / partition / government assignment), and conditions or liabilities attached. Under the Bhu Bharati Act — as under the 1971 Act before it — the state must keep it current, and a separate RoR is now also prepared for ABADI (village-site) and non-agricultural lands, stored electronically with certified copies available to anyone, including banks, on payment of a fee. Its legal engine is the PRESUMPTION OF TRUTH: every entry is presumed correct until the contrary is proved or the entry is lawfully amended. That presumption is why banks lend against the 1-B, why the registration system keys on it — and why a WRONG entry is so dangerous: the burden of proof sits on the person fighting the record, not the person enjoying it. Definition — Mode of acquisition: the 1-B’s one-word biography of the holding: how the current holder got it. “Purchase” points you to a deed to verify; “inheritance” points to a succession chain (all heirs? married daughters?); “government assignment” ends the conversation — that land cannot be sold to you. Example: The presumption, felt from both sides. FOR you: when your name is entered after clean mutation, anyone challenging your holding must PROVE you wrong — you start every dispute a goal up. AGAINST you: when a Dharani migration error spelled the owner’s name as someone else’s, the record’s presumption works for the WRONG name until corrected — which is precisely why the Act’s correction window (Part 7) exists, and why sleeping on a known error is legal self-harm. Example: The auto-update rule as a lie detector, worked: seller says “I bought this in 2019.” In Telangana, registration of a sale flows into the record — so the 1-B should show him from 2019. You pull it: pattadar is still the previous owner, mode of acquisition still “inheritance” from HIS father. Two possibilities only: the 2019 “purchase” was never registered (a sada bainama — see Part 7), or it does not exist. Either way, the state’s own register just cross-examined your seller in thirty seconds, free. Part 5 — Reading the two together: the disagreement playbook Professionals never read one record. They pull both, same day, and read the GAPS. Every gap has a canonical meaning: Pattern Most likely story Your move 1-B owner = seller; Pahani anubhavadar = someone else Tenant / adverse occupant in possession Resolve the occupant legally BEFORE price talk; long cultivation builds claims Pahani shows seller; 1-B shows older name Mutation never completed on some link Seller completes mutation first; never buy a promise to fix it later Both show a DEAD man Succession never filed Legal-heir certificate + succession mutation at the Tahsildar before anything; count the married daughters Extents differ between the two records Data-entry slip or an unrecorded partition RoR correction with old pahanis as proof — before the window closes 1-B says Patta; Pahani land-nature says Assigned/Sarkari A tampered or mistaken entry somewhere The restrictive reading wins until the record is formally corrected: treat as restricted, investigate at the MRO Crop columns empty for years on “farmed” land Nobody actually cultivates Fine for a plotting purchase — fatal for 54B/agricultural-income claims that need a farming record Example: Full worked example — one parcel, end to end. Target: 4-20 acres, Survey 172/B, near Shadnagar, quoted ₹1.1 crore/acre. Day 1, desk: 1-B — pattadar G. Lakshmamma w/o Malla Reddy, khata 88, mode: inheritance, extent 4-20, no liabilities. Pahani — anubhavadar G. Lakshmamma, nature Patta, classification Metta, borewell, cultivable 4-05 (15 guntas pote kharab: rocky), crops cotton for five faslis, liabilities: NIL. The two records AGREE. Day 2, ground: KYP at parcel centre matches 172/B; the woman in the fields is Lakshmamma’s daughter-in-law — consistent with family cultivation. Day 3, checks: 22A clean both portals, EC 30 years shows one released mortgage (2011 crop loan, discharged 2014 — matches a liabilities entry that later cleared). Diligence verdict: records coherent, price negotiable, the only file item is a succession consent from Lakshmamma’s children since mode = inheritance. THAT is what reading both records buys you: you now know the questions before the seller knows you have them. Part 6 — What the courts actually say (case by case, in plain words) This is where most buyers’ understanding is exactly backwards, so read slowly: the revenue record is strong evidence and weak title. The rulings, one by one: Ande Gagaiah v. M. Krishna Reddy (Telangana HC): entries in revenue records neither confer rights nor extinguish the rights of a true owner. Meaning: getting your name into the pahani does not MAKE you owner; a wrong entry does not UNMAKE the real one. Union of India v. Pramod Gupta (Supreme Court): no title can be claimed from a revenue entry — whoever claims ownership must prove the ownership was validly CONVEYED to them. Meaning: the entry is the shadow; the deed/grant is the object casting it. State of Haryana v. Amin Lal (Supreme Court): revenue entries do not confer title, BUT they are admissible evidence of possession and can support an ownership claim alongside other evidence. Meaning: the record is a witness — a good one — never the judgment. Sri Venkateshwara Developers v. Arepally Jeevan Rao (on Dharani itself): pahani entries on the portal are “not independently sustainable in law” — the portal is an administrative tool; courts decide on pleadings and instruments. Meaning: a Dharani/Bhu Bharati screenshot is not a trump card in litigation. V. Ramaswamy v. State of Telangana (Section 38-E, Tenancy Act 1950): the Tahsildar can vest OWNERSHIP in a protected tenant and restore possession — the one great exception where record-plus-statute genuinely creates title, which is why old sesala pahani tenant entries still matter. Definition — The three-layer model to keep: TITLE comes from instruments (registered deeds, grants, decrees, statutory vesting). RECORDS mirror title for administration and carry a rebuttable presumption. POSSESSION is fact on the ground, which records help prove. Confusing the layers is how buyers lose: they buy a record when they think they bought a title. Example: The layers in action: a man holds a 2005 registered sale deed (title layer) but never mutated; the pahani still names the seller (record layer); and the seller’s nephew has quietly farmed the parcel for 12 years (possession layer). Who wins what? The deed-holder likely wins TITLE — but fights an adverse-possession claim built on the record’s cultivation entries, and until mutation cannot cleanly sell or borrow. Three layers, three different fights. A pro keeps all three aligned at all times; that alignment is what “clean” means. Part 7 — Dharani’s wound and Bhu Bharati’s repair (the law you live under now) What went wrong, 2020–2024: the RoR Act 2020 fused registration and mutation into Dharani — genuinely fast — but the record was cut to a stub: the enjoyment column REMOVED, detail columns dropped, and mass migration errors put patta lands into “Part-B”, the blocked list, which swelled past 18 LAKH acres. Grievances had nowhere to go but civil courts, because the 2020 framework never even got implementing rules. Landowners could see their land vanish from the record and had no ladder to climb. What the 2025 Act does about it (passed December 2024; in force with Rules — GO Ms 39 — from 14 April 2025): Repair The mechanics Why you care Restored record 11-column Pahani back, enjoyment column back; separate RoR for abadi/non-agricultural land; village accounts (pahani, government land register, transfer register, irrigation register) maintained and filed yearly The record can again SHOW the disputes it used to hide Notice before amendment The Tahsildar must issue written notice to every affected person, publish it, hear objections, THEN amend The Dharani-era horror — waking up to a changed record — is now procedurally illegal The appeal ladder Tahsildar/Sub-Registrar order → RDO (60 days) → Collector (2nd appeal, 30 days) → LAND TRIBUNAL (final). Corrections on land worth over ₹5 lakh sit with the Collector directly Disputes climb an administrative ladder in weeks instead of civil courts in decades; free legal aid for farmers who cannot afford appeals Correction window Errors since 2020 correctable on application (≈₹1,000 fee) until 13 APRIL 2026; RDO-level enquiries with village evidence, orders targeted in 90 days One clean year to fix the migration’s damage — after which entries harden toward finality Sada bainama regularisation Old unregistered plain-paper sales (pre-2 June 2014) can be regularised on ground-level enquiry Lakhs of informal family-era transactions get a legal path into the record Succession discipline Family declaration + mandatory notices to ALL members before hereditary mutation; time-bound The one-heir-grabs-all mutation trick is structurally blocked Revision power (s.16) The Commissioner can reopen records of government, endowment, wakf, bhoodan and assigned lands changed FRAUDULENTLY Fraudulent entries on protected categories are never safe, however old Bhudhaar spine Every parcel auto-assigned its GPS-anchored unique ID; passbook-cum-title-deed issued against the record The identity system the previous classes covered — this Act is where it is born Example: The ladder, worked: a Siddipet farmer finds his 3-10 acres recorded as 2-10 after migration. Old path (2021): a civil suit, ₹50,000+ in fees, five-plus years. New path: correction application with the 1989 passbook and khasra pahani attached (~₹1,000) → Tahsildar/RDO enquiry with neighbours → order targeted inside 90 days; if refused, RDO appeal within 60 days, then Collector, then Tribunal — each rung time-bound. The substance of his case is identical; the SYSTEM around it is transformed. That is what a records statute is actually for. Example: The deadline, worked backwards: it is late August 2026 in this paper’s world — the 13 April 2026 window has CLOSED for casual corrections. What survives? Appeals up the ladder, the s.16 revision route for fraud on protected lands, and civil remedies. The lesson for every future window (and there will be others as the resurvey lands): the state occasionally opens a door that turns litigation into paperwork. Professionals walk through doors while they are open — the previous RoR-correction class exists because we watched this one close. Part 8 — The fraud museum (real cases from the state’s own audit) These are not hypotheticals. India’s national auditor (CAG) examined Telangana’s land records and published what it found — each finding is a masterclass in how record systems fail: The 500 phantom acres (Shamshabad): the khasra pahani showed survey number 62 of Bahadurguda holding 500 acres of GOVERNMENT land. The tippan and village map showed SN 62 physically smaller than five neighbouring numbers totalling ~63 acres — and the Tahsildar confirmed the 500 acres did not physically exist. Government land worth ₹24.42 crore, unaccounted, because three records that should agree never did. Lesson: extent claims are checked against the MAP records (tippan/FMB), not just other text records. The tampered khasra (SN 65): a survey number recorded as 547-27 acres was sub-divided into 33 parts; departmental enquiry found the 1954-55 khasra pahani itself had been TAMPERED with — wrong entries written into the foundation record — and title stayed unsettled decades later. Lesson: even the “root” record can be corrupted; multi-generation cross-checking (sethwar vs khasra vs current) is how tampering surfaces. The reclassified government land (Alwal): 16 acres classified as maqtha (a government-linked category) in the sesala pahani appeared as PATTA land in the 2013-14 pahani — and occupants then claimed ownership from the newer entry. Lesson: a favourable NEW entry against an unfavourable OLD one is a red flag pointing backwards, not a windfall. The drifting village (Rameshwarpally): between the sethwar and the pahani, 83 survey numbers showed 122 MORE acres in the pahani and 36 showed 14 FEWER. A whole village whose two core records disagree by over a hundred acres. Lesson: extent errors are systemic, not exotic — which is why resurveys and the LPM exist. The half-done mutation (Cheeryal): five sons inherited; the mutation was carried into the RoR 1-B but never into the pahani for years. Lesson: mutation is not done when ONE record updates — it is done when BOTH do. Check both after every transaction, including your own. Example: Turn the museum into a checklist: (1) map records against text records for extent; (2) oldest layer against newest for classification and nature; (3) both current records against each other after every mutation; (4) any too-good newer entry investigated backwards. Four habits, each born from a real failure above — this is what “learning from other people’s disasters” literally looks like. Part 9 — Getting the records (the practical mechanics, complete) Free online view: bhubharati.telangana.gov.in (agricultural; Dharani redirects here) or ccla.telangana.gov.in → Land Details Search → district, mandal, village → search by survey/sub-division number, khata, passbook number, or name (see the name-search class). Read on screen, download, print — research grade only. Certified copies (the legal grade): MeeSeva in the land’s own mandal — Pahani ₹35, RoR 1-B ₹25, about 15 minutes for current records; the Act guarantees certified extracts to ANY applicant including banks. Digitally signed portal copies carry QR + Bhudhaar (see the certified-copy class). Old records (khasra pahani, sesala pahani, old faslis): apply at the Tahsildar’s office — days, not minutes, and worth every day when a correction or dispute is live. The urban split: agricultural records live here; EC, market value and deed copies live on IGRS (registration.telangana.gov.in) — the two-portal rule from the hub class. Example: The ₹95 full stack: certified Pahani (₹35) + certified 1-B (₹25) + a fresh signed portal PDF (~₹35 equivalent fee). For less than a hundred rupees and one MeeSeva visit you hold the complete, bank-grade, current truth about any parcel in Telangana. There is no cheaper professional edge in Indian real estate. Part 10 — The glossary (speak the record’s language) Term Meaning Pahani / Adangal The annual village cultivation-and-holding record (Village Account 3) RoR 1-B The ownership extract of the Record of Rights Pattadar The recorded holder liable for land revenue Anubhavadar / sagu The “enjoyer” — actual occupant/cultivator Khata The holder’s account grouping their parcels in a village Khatadar The person to whom the khata belongs Tari / Metta Wet (irrigated) / dry (rain-fed) land Shikam Tank-bed land — flood-prone, restricted, frequent litigation Poramboke Government/common land — roads, riverbeds, grazing; never privately saleable Pote kharab The unusable portion inside a parcel (rocks, paths, nala) Inam / maqtha / jagir Nizam-era grant tenures, abolished post-1948 — legacy entries that still complicate titles Kharij khata An account struck off / held in abeyance — investigate before touching Sada bainama An unregistered plain-paper sale — regularisable (pre-June-2014) under the new Act Fasli The revenue year (≈ calendar year + 590) Jamabandi The annual closing/audit of village accounts at fasli-end Sethwar / tippan / wasool baqi Settlement register / field sketch / old-to-new survey correlation register Example: Why vocabulary is leverage: at a Tahsildar counter, “the record is wrong” gets a shrug; “the pahani’s anubhavadar column contradicts the 1-B and the khasra pahani of fasli 1364 — I want a correction under the Act with these certified copies attached” gets a file opened. Officials triage by fluency. So do sellers. Quick answers (FAQ) Which one proves ownership? Neither, by itself — courts are unanimous. The 1-B carries a presumption; title lives in registered instruments. Keep deed + 1-B + Pahani aligned and the question never bites. How current is each? Pahani: every fasli (and on transactions); 1-B: on every registered transaction/mutation. Are Dharani-era entries trustworthy? Treat 2020–2025 entries as the error-prone layer — verify against pre-2020 paper where stakes are high. What are the exact fees? View free; certified Pahani ₹35, 1-B ₹25; corrections ≈ ₹1,000 (window now closed — appeals remain). Can I get someone else’s records? Yes — the Act makes certified extracts available to all applicants; land records are public by design. What single habit captures this whole masterclass? Pull BOTH records, same day, before every conversation about any parcel — and file dated copies every time. Bottom line Two books, one truth — when they agree. The Pahani tells you what the land IS this year; the 1-B tells you WHOSE it has been across years; the courts tell you neither is title but both are evidence; history tells you the older layers are your ammunition; and the new Act finally gives you a ladder when the books are wrong. Master these two documents and every other Telangana land record — EC, passbook, Bhudhaar, map — becomes a footnote to a story you already know how to read. For you: Institutionalise this: (1) a per-parcel “record file” — dated certified Pahani + 1-B at acquisition, at every loan, at listing, and every jamabandi (fasli-end) as an annual audit of your whole land bank; (2) the disagreement playbook (Part 5) printed for your team — gaps between the two records ARE the due-diligence findings; (3) for JD sourcing, the khata trick — one khata search shows a family’s entire village holding before they choose what to tell you; (4) when any dispute stirs, go OLD first: khasra pahani, sesala, sethwar — the record generations that outrank whatever a portal shows today. The developer who reads both books faster than the market prices them owns the corridor. Original Deccan Ledger deep-research masterclass; sources below. tg-pahani-ror1b: Key Highlights Pahani (Adangal) records the physical facts — owner, use, soil, survey number; RoR 1-B records the legal title, khata and the full ownership history. Issued by the Tahsildar; free to view online; certified copies ₹35 (Pahani) / ₹25 (RoR 1-B) at MeeSeva, ready in ~15 minutes. The Bhu Bharati Act 2025 replaced Dharani for agricultural land: 11-column Pahani, GPS-linked LPM numbers, mandatory annual updates. RoR 1-B auto-updates the moment a sale deed registers — a seller whose “years-old purchase” still shows the old name never registered it. Walk away. The online view is for research; only the certified copy works for banks, courts and registration. What the two records are Pahani — also called Adangal — is the Tahsildar’s record of a parcel’s PHYSICAL facts: who owns it, how it is used, the soil type, the survey number. RoR 1-B — the Record of Rights — is the village-wise OWNERSHIP register: legal title, khata number, and the full history of who held the land and how it changed hands. The simplest frame: Pahani tells you what the land IS; RoR 1-B tells you who it BELONGS to. You need both before you talk price with anyone. Definition — Khata number: the revenue account number under which a holder’s parcels are grouped in the village register — the “account” the land sits in, distinct from the survey number which identifies the parcel itself. How Telangana’s record system evolved Digitisation began in the Maa Bhoomi era; Dharani took over in 2020 and put everything under one portal; and in 2025 the state passed the Bhu Bharati (Record of Rights in Land) Act , replacing Dharani for agricultural land with a tighter system — restored 11-column Pahani entries, GPS-linked parcel identifiers called LPM (Land Parcel Map) numbers, and mandatory annual updates. Dharani’s records were thin; Bhu Bharati mostly fixes that, though the transition has left data gaps worth knowing about. How to check them (online, free) Keep district, mandal, village and the survey/khata number ready — the search will not run without at least one. 1) Open dharani.telangana.gov.in or ccla.telangana.gov.in (both official; avoid third-party sites selling “reports” of a free record). 2) Click “Know Your Land Status” → “Pahani and ROR-1B” under Records of Rights. 3) Pick district, division, mandal, village; search by survey number, khata number, name or mutation date; captcha; Get Details. 4) Read, download, print — good for YOUR research, not for a court or bank file. Getting certified copies (MeeSeva) For any official purpose — loan, dispute, registration — the certified copy is the only version that counts. Go to the MeeSeva centre in the SAME mandal as the land (a different district’s MeeSeva has no jurisdiction); ask for the Adangal form (Pahani) or RoR 1-B application; pay ₹35 / ₹25; the operator issues a receipt with an application number (also sent to your mobile — keep it for tracking); collect in about 15 minutes. Pre-digitisation records are a separate application at the Tahsildar office and can take days. Reading the RoR 1-B, field by field Field What it means What to check Khatadar’s name Legal owner in the revenue register Identical to the seller’s name on the deed — even a spelling variant is worth clarifying Survey / LPM number Parcel ID tied to the cadastral map Stand on the land and confirm boundaries; Bhu Bharati registrations now run on LPM numbers Extent Area in acres and guntas Match the deed; independently measure when the numbers are close but not exact Land classification Wet, Dry, Garden, Shikam, Waste Decides legal use; agricultural land needs NALA conversion before construction Mode of acquisition Purchase / inheritance / government assignment “Government Assignment” is a HARD STOP — that land cannot be sold Liabilities / encumbrances Bank loans, mortgages, attachment orders Any entry = a live claim on the title; do not buy until cleared Good sign: one owner name throughout, no liabilities, classification matching the seller’s story, and an LPM that lines up with the parcel when you stand on it. Common problems and the fix Name on RoR doesn’t match the deed — mutation never happened; the SELLER completes mutation at the Tahsildar BEFORE you sign anything; never accept “we’ll fix it after”. Multiple names on one survey number — a paper partition never carried into the record; get the partition documents and a lawyer’s confirmation of each share; one missing co-owner signature kills the sale. Mode of acquisition says Government Assignment — stop; no instrument cures it. Example: The auto-update rule is a built-in lie detector: RoR 1-B refreshes the moment a sale registers in Telangana. A seller claiming he bought the parcel in 2019 while the record still names his vendor is telling you — in the government’s own handwriting — that the purchase was never registered. Quick answers (FAQ) Are Pahani and RoR 1-B the same? Linked, not the same — cultivation facts vs ownership title; read both. Cost? Free online; ₹35/₹25 certified at MeeSeva. Validity? Current financial year; refreshes after every registered transaction. Which portal? dharani.telangana.gov.in / ccla.telangana.gov.in (agricultural records moving to Bhu Bharati). Bottom line Two free searches and ₹60 of certified copies tell you who owns the land, what it legally is, and what claims ride on it — before the first price conversation. Refuse any deal where the record and the seller’s story disagree. For you: Make the Pahani + 1-B pull the FIRST act of every parcel conversation — before the site visit, before pricing. And flip it into sales: pull both records live in front of YOUR plot buyers; the developer who opens the portal unasked is the developer whose word needs no checking. tg-passbook: Key Highlights The Pattadar Passbook (PPB / e-Passbook / “Title Deed”) is Telangana’s primary ownership document for agricultural land, under the Rights in Land and Pattadar Passbooks Act, 2020. Aadhaar-linked: it carries the owner’s photo, thumbprint and biometric identity — built to kill impersonation fraud. Every bank in the state demands it before any agricultural loan. It is SEPARATE from the sale deed — after purchase it must be transferred into your name via mutation; a deed without an updated Passbook is a legal grey zone. The documented fraud: buyers who skip mutation have had previous owners RE-MUTATE the land under succession claims. Agricultural registration in Telangana requires the buyer IN PERSON with biometrics — no GPA stand-ins. What the Passbook is The Revenue Department’s Aadhaar-linked record of who holds title to agricultural land — proof of legal ownership before any court, bank or department, recording the full ownership history against the parcel. Most buyers know they need a sale deed; fewer know the Passbook is a separate document that must be TRANSFERRED into their name afterwards through mutation. The deed registers the transaction; the Passbook is what the revenue system recognises. Hold a deed without the updated Passbook and government schemes, bank loans and any onward sale all hit a wall. Definition — Pattadar: the recorded holder of the patta — the person the state’s register names as owner. The Passbook is the pattadar’s identity-linked certificate of that status. The anti-fraud design The Passbook carries photograph, thumbprint and Aadhaar-verified identity precisely so a stranger cannot pose as the owner. Two consequences for buyers: if the face in the seller’s Passbook is not the face across the table, investigate before signing anything; and under the RoR Act 2020, a Passbook fraudulently created for GOVERNMENT land can be cancelled by the District Collector, with criminal proceedings and resumption of the land — a Passbook is strong evidence, not an unconditional guarantee. How to check one (free, online) 1) Open dharani.telangana.gov.in or bhubharati.telangana.gov.in — Bhu Bharati is the updated portal under the 2025 Act and has the more current agricultural records. 2) No login needed to view; open the search screen. 3) Select district, mandal, village; search by Passbook number (faster — pulls the full record) or survey number; have the first four digits of the linked Aadhaar ready. 4) Verify owner name, Aadhaar linkage, survey number, extent, land type, transaction history; download. The online view verifies; banks want the MRO-signed hard copy. Getting it transferred after YOU buy 1) Attend registration in person — agricultural registration under the Telangana system needs the buyer’s physical presence and biometric verification; both sides appear; no General Power of Attorney stand-in. 2) Mutation is typically AUTOMATIC after registration; if it does not trigger, apply via the portal’s citizen services or at the Tahsildar with documents. 3) When mutation processes, check the new Passbook on the portal field by field — name, survey number, extent, Aadhaar. 4) The physical Passbook posts to your address after Tahsildar approval; track by application number. Lost one? Duplicate at the MRO with Aadhaar-linked mobile verification. What the Passbook contains Field What it means What to check Pattadar name + photo Aadhaar-linked identity of the owner The face must match the seller — a photo mismatch on a biometric document is a serious red flag Aadhaar number Linked identity number Cross-check against the seller’s physical ID Survey + khata number Parcel and account identifiers Verify against boundaries and the deed — errors cascade into every later transaction Extent Area in acres/guntas Must match the deed; small discrepancies need a correction order BEFORE registration Land type Wet / Dry / other Drives loan eligibility and permitted use — read the column, not the seller’s description Transaction & mutation history Every recorded ownership change Recent, frequent activity deserves entry-by-entry scrutiny The documented fraud pattern The most recorded scam under Dharani: a buyer registers the sale but delays mutation — the revenue record still names the previous owner, who then applies for mutation AGAIN under succession or other grounds, effectively reclaiming the Passbook. Thousands of genuine buyers have faced this. The rule is absolute: mutation immediately after registration — even a week’s delay is a window. Example: Sequence for every purchase: register (in person, biometric) → confirm auto-mutation triggered the same week → verify the new e-Passbook online → receive the physical book → THEN treat the purchase as complete. The deal is not done at the SRO; it is done when the Passbook says your name. Quick answers (FAQ) Is the Passbook the same as the sale deed? No — deed records the transaction, Passbook records recognised ownership; you need both, in your name. Cost? Free to view online; duplicates via the MRO. Expiry? None — it updates after every registered transaction. Why do banks insist on it? It is the state’s biometric-verified title record — the cleanest collateral check that exists here. Bottom line In Telangana the Passbook IS ownership as the state sees it. Verify the seller’s before you pay; chase your own the week you register; and treat any gap between deed and Passbook as a live risk, because the fraudsters certainly do. For you: For your JD assemblies: every landowner partner’s Passbook should be pulled and face-matched at the first meeting — it kills the two worst surprises (imposters, and un-mutated inheritors who cannot yet sign). And when your buyers’ ventures involve farm plots, walking them through their own Passbook transfer converts a legal chore into a loyalty moment. tg-adangal: Key Highlights Adangal (Pahani / Village Account) records cultivation: soil, crops, irrigation, tenancy, classification — Part II of the Record of Rights, updated annually by the MRO. RoR 1-B is legal title; Adangal is ACTUAL USE — and a tenant in years-long occupation is a dispute no sale deed erases. The wet / dry / waste classification is the field buyers ignore and sellers count on them ignoring — price follows the column, not the pitch. Land Nature must read PATTA to be privately transferable — Sarkari = government land; Assigned = welfare land that cannot be sold to you. Free on Dharani/CCLA; ₹35 certified copy at MeeSeva. What the Adangal is The Tahsildar’s cultivation register for every agricultural parcel in a village: who cultivates, what crops, which soil, what irrigation source, whether a tenant is involved, and the land’s classification. It functions as Part II of the Record of Rights — the cultivation side of the same system the RoR 1-B’s title side belongs to. People treat the two as interchangeable; they are not. For a buyer, the Adangal often reveals what the title record keeps quiet. Definition — Fasli: the revenue year used in cultivation records. The Adangal’s crop entries are recorded fasli by fasli — a parcel’s recent faslis show who has actually been farming it. The classification money hides in Wet land is irrigated — commands higher prices, faces stricter use restrictions. Dry is rain-fed. Waste has no cultivation history — and in Telangana sometimes turns out to have no legal private ownership at all. Before agreeing any price, open the Adangal and read the Land Nature and classification columns yourself: the seller’s valuation often assumes a classification the document does not support. How to get it Online (free): dharani.telangana.gov.in or ccla.telangana.gov.in → “Land Details Search” / “Know Your Land Status → Pahani and ROR-1B” → district, division, mandal, village → search by survey, khata or linked Aadhaar → captcha → read the Land Nature column FIRST, then the cultivator name against the seller’s. Certified (₹35): MeeSeva in the land’s own mandal; application number to your mobile; ~15 minutes for current records — and insist on the MRO-signed version; an unsigned printout has no official weight. Pre-digitisation Adangals: apply at the Tahsildar, allow days. Reading it, field by field Field What it means What to check Survey / hissa number Parcel ID Cross-check site and cadastral map — mismatch = boundary risk Khatadar name Registered pattadar Must match the seller exactly — mismatch means mutation never completed Land classification Wet, Dry, Garden, Shikam, Waste Sets legal use and honest value — read it yourself Land Nature Patta / Sarkari / Assigned Patta transfers privately; Sarkari and Assigned do NOT — one word can end the deal Crops & cultivation Last fasli’s crops, irrigation, tenancy Reveals active tenants with possession claims; also drives crop-loan / PMFBY eligibility Soil classification Soil type and water rate Feeds productivity value and the bank’s assessment Good sign: Land Nature = Patta, khatadar = seller, no tenant in the cultivator column, classification consistent with the pitch, survey number pulling up clean. The traps, with fixes Assigned sold as private — welfare land distributed to landless farmers cannot be sold, full stop; corridor sellers around Hyderabad routinely pitch assigned parcels as investments; the Adangal exposes it — the moment you see Assigned, stop; any deed on it is void from execution. Active tenant in the cultivator column — someone else has been farming, possibly for years; long cultivation creates de facto possession claims in Telangana courts; get a legal opinion on the tenancy BEFORE agreeing anything. Waste priced as wet — verify classification on the portal before any price talk. Old khatadar name — mutation never filed; seller fixes it at the Tahsildar first. Forged offline Adangal — documented cases include fake cultivation records supporting fraudulent sales (one disputed patta parcel was sold as a 43-plot venture with no planning approval); pull the survey number on the portal YOURSELF and compare every field. Example: The one-word audit: open the Adangal, read Land Nature. “Patta” — continue the conversation. “Sarkari” or “Assigned” — the conversation is over, at any discount, with any paperwork. Quick answers (FAQ) Adangal vs Pahani? Same document, two names. Adangal vs RoR 1-B? Use vs title — read both. Cost? Free online; ₹35 certified. Why does a plotting buyer care about crops? Because tenancy, classification and Land Nature decide whether the parcel can ever legally become plots. Bottom line The Adangal is the cheapest lie detector in Telangana land: one free search shows the tenant the seller forgot to mention, the classification the price ignores, and the one word — Assigned — that no lawyer can fix. For you: Add a fixed “Adangal line” to your parcel checklist: Land Nature / cultivator vs seller / classification vs pitch. Ten seconds per parcel, and it catches the two deal-killers (assigned taint, sitting tenant) earlier than any title search. tg-mother-deed: Key Highlights The Mother Deed (Mula Deed / Parent Document / Root of Title) is the FIRST registered document that established ownership — every later deed links back to it. Only a registered deed transfers title (Registration Act 1908 + TP Act 1882); an unregistered instrument is inadmissible under Section 49. Certified copies: ₹200 each; online 1–2 days via IGRS; manual SRO copies 10–15 working days. IGRS holds digitised deeds from 1 Jan 1983 ONLY — older transfers need a manual index-book search at the SRO. A blank portal result is NOT a clean title. Supreme Court (SLP (C) 1866/2024, decided 7 May 2025): a registered sale deed alone does not guarantee ownership if the seller’s underlying title is defective. What the Mother Deed is Telangana’s property market runs on what the Registration Department calls LINK documents. The Mother Deed — locally the Mula Deed — is the start of that chain: the moment a property first entered registered ownership, through a government grant, revenue patta, court decree, partition or sale. Every gift, sale or settlement afterwards connects back to it. Buyers confuse the Mula Deed with the LATEST sale deed; they are different things — one root per property, many branches accumulating over decades. A 30-year title search begins at the root and traces every transfer forward; a missing or broken link anywhere is a serious defect. Definition — Link document: any registered deed forming one link in the ownership chain between the Mother Deed and today’s seller. Banks asking for “link documents” want the whole chain, not just the newest deed. Checking the chain online (IGRS) 1) Create a Citizen account on registration.telangana.gov.in — Aadhaar-linked mobile, name spelled EXACTLY as on Aadhaar (variations cause download mismatches). 2) Open Deed Details / Certified Copy services → district → SRO → document number + year → Get Details; a second no-login cross-check runs at ccla.telangana.gov.in/deedDetailsWs.do. 3) Verify EVERY field against the physical deed: document number character by character; nature of deed (a sale deed and an agreement of sale are NOT the same); executant and claimant names vs Aadhaar; survey number, extent, boundaries, village, mandal — one mismatch needs explaining before you proceed. 4) Pay ₹200 per certified copy; the digitally signed PDF arrives in 1–2 days with full legal weight. Note: agricultural-land records are moving to the Bhu Bharati portal — confirm which portal covers your property type first. The pre-1983 trap and the offline route IGRS digitisation starts at 1 January 1983. Older transfers exist only in physical index books — so a blank portal result on an old property means “search manually”, never “clean”. Offline: 1) find the correct SRO — jurisdiction follows the PROPERTY, though since a 2024 update Hyderabad city buyers may use any of the 11 city SROs (Banjara Hills, Charminar, Secunderabad…); 2) submit a written application with document number, approximate year, parties, survey number — for pre-1983, specifically request the manual index-book search; 3) fees: ₹200 per certified copy; EC to 30 years ₹200, beyond ₹500; carry Aadhaar and any existing deed; 4) manual certified copies take 10–15 working days and carry the sub-registrar’s seal — fully admissible in banks and courts. What a registered deed must show Field What it refers to Why it matters Document number + year SRO identifier at registration Must match the paper deed exactly — one character off is a fraud signal Nature of deed Sale / Gift / Partition / Settlement / Court decree A registered SALE DEED transfers title; an agreement of sale does not Executant & claimant Seller and buyer legal names Cross-check Aadhaar; deeds from 2001 on carry photos + thumbprints (s.32A) Property schedule Survey no., extent, all four boundaries Must match the ground — hire a surveyor if measurements differ at all Mode of acquisition How the seller got title Traces the link into the chain above it Why the chain outranks the newest deed The Supreme Court’s 2025 ruling says it plainly: a registered sale deed does NOT guarantee ownership when the seller’s own title is defective. Registration certifies the transaction happened — not that the transferor had anything to transfer. That is why the lawyer’s 30-year search exists, and why it starts at the Mula Deed instead of the latest photocopy. Example: A Shankarpally parcel: clean 2016 sale deed, verified on IGRS. The chain search finds the 1998 link was a partition deed one brother executed for land the family never actually partitioned — every deed after it inherits the defect. The 2016 paper was genuine; the title behind it was not. The root decides. Quick answers (FAQ) Is the Mother Deed one document? Yes — one per property; everything else is links. How far should the search go? 30 years standard, always reaching the root. What does a certified copy cost? ₹200 (online 1–2 days; manual 10–15 days). Portal shows nothing? If pre-1983 — manual search; never assume clean. Bottom line Buy the chain, not the deed. Root to today, link by link, every field matched — with the manual index books doing the years the portal cannot see. For you: Your acquisition rule: no agreement until the chain file (Mula Deed → every link → today) sits complete in YOUR folder, not promised from the seller’s. And archive your ventures’ complete chains digitally — the developer who hands a buyer’s bank the full link set in one PDF closes loans weeks faster than the market. tg-bb-land-details: Key Highlights The restored 11-column Pahani shows pattadar, extent, classification, mode of acquisition AND the enjoyment column; the 1B is the ownership extract drawn from it. The ENJOYMENT column records who actually occupies and cultivates — a mismatch with the seller is the classic sign of a tenancy or possession dispute. Search runs on three identifiers: old survey number, new LPM (drone resurvey), Bhudhaar — if one fails, try the next before assuming the record is missing. Viewing is free; banks and registrars accept ONLY the digitally signed PDF with QR and Bhudhaar. Registration itself now runs on this record — the slot will not open without a verified Bhudhaar. What the record shows The Pahani (village account) and RoR 1B are Telangana’s core land records, and Bhu Bharati’s restored 11-column format returns the detail Dharani stripped out. Most people read the owner name and stop; the land’s legal health lives in the columns beside it. Two matter most for buyers: enjoyment — who actually occupies and cultivates (mismatch = presume a possession dispute until proven otherwise); and mode of acquisition — government-assigned land carries transfer restrictions no sale deed can cure. Definition — Enjoyment column: the Pahani’s record of actual occupation — who is physically on and farming the parcel, as distinct from who holds title. The gap between the two names is where tenancy claims live. How to check, step by step Online: 1) bhubharati.telangana.gov.in — register with mobile + OTP, using the SAME name spelling as your documents so later transactions don’t bounce. 2) Land Details Search → Pahani or ROR 1B → district, mandal, village (wrong village is the top reason searches return nothing). 3) Enter survey number, LPM or Bhudhaar + captcha; if the survey number fails, switch to the LPM printed on the Pattadar Passbook — resurveyed parcels often answer to it first. 4) View free; pay the small fee for the digitally signed PDF with QR and Bhudhaar — screenshots and plain printouts are rejected by banks and registrars. Offline: MRO with the survey number or Passbook; request the SIGNED copy, not a photocopy of a screen; MeeSeva prints are fine for a first look only. Field-by-field reading Field What it means What to check Pattadar name Recorded owner Matches seller and deed exactly, spelling included Extent Area of the holding Tallies with deed and physical measurement Classification Wet, dry, shikam + soil data Sets permitted use, value, conversion needs Enjoyment Who occupies / cultivates Mismatch = possession dispute signal Mode of acquisition Inheritance / purchase / assignment Assigned = transfer restrictions; trace it Bhudhaar / LPM Parcel identifiers Both must point at the exact parcel you are buying Good sign: the record loads instantly, downloads as a signed PDF with QR and Bhudhaar, and shows an enjoyment column matching the seller. The four stuck-search failures, and fixes “No records found” — usually migration lag (often mid-NALA sync), rarely deletion: search by the Passbook’s LPM, retry in days, then the MRO. Record not digitally signed — invalid for sale or loan: ask the MRO to apply the Tahsildar’s signature. Survey number stops working — re-mapped to an LPM in the drone resurvey: find the LPM via the passbook and search with that. Name carried over wrong — a Dharani-era spelling error that quietly blocks loans and registration: file RoR correction at the Tahsildar before the 13 April 2026 deadline. Why this record decides the deal Telangana has tied REGISTRATION itself to this record: the slot will not open without a verified Bhudhaar, and every lender pulls the Pahani before sanctioning a plot or farm loan. Read it twice — once online before the site visit, once ON SITE against what you see; the column that disagrees with reality is the one that costs lakhs later. Example: The live-pull test: ask the seller to open the record on the portal in front of you. A seller who refuses, or explains away an enjoyment mismatch verbally, has answered your due-diligence question — walk away. Quick answers (FAQ) Pahani vs 1B? Full 11-column record vs the ownership extract — read both. Free? Viewing yes; the signed PDF costs a small fee. Survey number shows nothing? Probably re-mapped — use the LPM. Which copy do banks accept? Only the signed PDF with QR and Bhudhaar. Bottom line The record IS the deal now — registration and lending both run on it. A clean, signed, ground-matching Pahani is not paperwork; it is the asset. For you: Standardise the two-read ritual across your team: portal read before the site visit, printed record IN HAND during it, enjoyment column checked against whoever is standing on the land. The question “then who is that farming it?” has saved more Telangana buyers than any lawyer’s opinion. Original Deccan Ledger guide lesson; full source guide on 1acre.in (links above). tg-bb-certified-copy: Key Highlights The certified copy = the Pahani/1B as a digitally signed PDF under the Tahsildar’s signature, with QR code and Bhudhaar embedded. It is the ONLY version accepted for loans, registration and legal proceedings — screenshots and plain printouts are rejected outright. Two preconditions: the underlying record must be signed, and its details must match your deed exactly. The fee is small and per-copy; lenders want a FRESH download near any transaction. Anyone selling to “arrange” a certified copy off-portal for a premium is selling a free download — or a forgery. Why only the signed copy counts The logic is anti-fraud: a screenshot can be edited in minutes, while a signed PDF is cryptographically tied to the record and its QR lets anyone verify it against the portal in seconds — so institutions stopped accepting anything less. Two things must be true for your download to work: the record itself carries the Tahsildar’s digital signature, and the details match your deed to the character. An unsigned record produces an unsigned copy — the single most common rejection at loan scrutiny. Downloading it Online: 1) pull the Pahani/1B on bhubharati.telangana.gov.in (survey number, LPM or Bhudhaar) and confirm every field BEFORE paying; 2) choose the CERTIFIED option, not the plain view; 3) pay the statutory fee, download the signed PDF, save the payment reference with the file; 4) scan the QR yourself and confirm it resolves to the same record — before handing it to anyone. Offline: MRO/MeeSeva counter — insist on the signed version (a stamped photocopy of a screen is not a certified copy) and scan the QR before leaving the counter. What banks check on the copy Check Why it matters Fail means Digital signature valid Ties the copy to the Tahsildar Rejected outright QR resolves to portal Copy is live and unedited Treated as forged Bhudhaar present Links copy to the exact parcel Identity of the land in doubt Name matches deed Spelling-level comparison Loan stalls on discrepancy Recent download date Institutions want current state Asked to re-pull Common failures, and fixes Certified-copy problems are really RECORD problems. Comes back unsigned — the signature was never applied: request it at the MRO, then re-download. QR fails or mismatches — stale/tampered copy or sync lag: re-download fresh; persisting mismatch goes to the MRO. Name differs from deed — Dharani-era spelling error surfacing at the worst time: file RoR correction before the 2026 deadline, then re-download. Bhudhaar shows temporary — parcel-ID verification incomplete: pursue permanent status first; institutions increasingly check it. When to pull a fresh copy Three moments, always: before LISTING land for sale; before any LOAN application; and within two weeks AFTER registration — to confirm mutation carried your name in correctly. Keep the copies dated and filed: a trail of signed PDFs across time is quiet, powerful evidence if a dispute ever asks what the record said, and when. Example: ₹45 of downloads over three years — at purchase, at loan, at listing — is a complete, timestamped, government-signed history of your parcel. The cheapest litigation insurance in Telangana. Quick answers (FAQ) What makes a copy “certified”? Tahsildar’s digital signature + QR + Bhudhaar in one PDF. Do banks take plain printouts? Never. How do I verify a copy someone hands me? Scan its QR; if it doesn’t resolve to the same record, it is worthless. How recent must it be? Fresh near any transaction — current state, not last year’s snapshot. Bottom line One habit covers everything: never transact on an unsigned record, and never trust a copy whose QR you have not scanned yourself. For you: Build the dated-PDF archive for every parcel you hold — purchase, loan, listing, plus an annual pull. And when selling plots, hand each buyer a fresh signed copy in their closing kit: it pre-answers the bank’s first question and marks you as the venture whose records are always transaction-ready. tg-bb-name-search: Key Highlights Name search finds records by the pattadar’s recorded name within ONE village — a shortlist tool, never proof. Three uses: inherited land where the family knows the village but not the survey number; lost-document holdings; and checking how much a SELLER really owns in a village. Rural Telangana repeats names heavily, and spellings differ across Aadhaar, passbook and record — search every variant. It runs village by village: the right name in the WRONG village returns nothing, which buyers misread as “no holdings”. Confirm every hit with father’s name → extent → khata → survey/LPM → Bhudhaar before relying on anything. When to search by name Three situations make it invaluable: inherited land — the family knows the village, nobody knows the survey number; old holdings whose papers are lost; and pre-purchase checks on how much land a seller actually holds where they claim to. The catch is precision: names repeat, transliterations drift, and a search under one spelling can miss the record filed under another. Treat every result as a shortlist to be confirmed, never a conclusion. How to run it Online (free): 1) bhubharati.telangana.gov.in → Land Details Search → record type → district, mandal, VILLAGE (it only runs inside one village at a time); 2) switch to search-by-name; enter the name as on the passbook or old records — retry Telugu-style and English transliterations, initials expanded and contracted; 3) scan the rows, shortlisting by father’s name and expected extent (common names return dozens); 4) open the shortlisted record and NOTE its survey number, LPM and Bhudhaar — all future checks run on those, never on the name. Offline: the MRO’s pattadar index allows more spelling flexibility than the portal — carry the passbook, Aadhaar or an old Pahani, and leave with identifiers written down, not just a nod. Narrowing common names Discriminator Where it appears What it settles Father’s name Record and passbook Separates namesakes within a village Extent Record Matches the claimed holding size Khata number Record Groups all parcels under one holder Survey no / LPM Record and map Pins the exact parcel on the ground Bhudhaar Record Final, unique confirmation Good sign: a shortlisted record whose father’s name, extent and khata all agree with the documents in front of you — confirmed by LPM. The four predictable failures, and fixes Too many identical names — filter by father’s name and extent, confirm by LPM. Spelling variant misses — retry transliterations. Holder is deceased — records keep the late pattadar’s name until mutation completes: for inherited land, expect the grandfather’s or father’s name, then check mutation status. Zero results — usually the wrong village (boundaries also moved in the resurvey): confirm the current revenue village at the MRO and search again. Why buyers run it even with the survey number in hand A name search on the SELLER shows every parcel they hold in the village — which closes the neighbouring-parcel trick, where a clean parcel is shown and a disputed neighbouring one is registered. For inherited land it is step one of a chain: locate the record → check whether mutation moved it to the heirs → only then discuss any sale. Example: Red-flag test: a seller who resists a simple name search of their own holdings — or whose claimed land appears under NO spelling in the stated village — is not ready for your advance. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I find land with just a name? Yes — free, within a chosen village. Search shows nothing — is the land unrecorded? Not necessarily: try variants, confirm the village, check whether it still stands in a deceased relative’s name. Is a name match enough to buy on? Never — confirm survey number, LPM and Bhudhaar. Can I see everything one person owns? Within one village, effectively yes; statewide views are not public — repeat per village. Bottom line Name search opens the door; identifiers close the deal. Use it to FIND records and audit sellers — then switch immediately to survey/LPM/Bhudhaar for everything that matters. For you: Two professional uses: audit every landowner partner’s FULL village holdings before a JD (their other parcels’ disputes have a way of visiting yours), and use it in land-buying negotiations — knowing the family holds 12 acres nearby, not just the 2 being discussed, changes what you offer and how. tg-bhu-naksha: Key Highlights Bhu Naksha (cadastral map / survey sketch / Tippon offline) shows every parcel’s shape, boundary and area on one GIS view — under the Survey and Boundaries Act 1923, now the Bhu Bharati Act 2025. The 2025 statewide DRONE survey rebuilt the map from scratch — every parcel flown, photographed, tied to GPS — creating the LPM number alongside the old survey number. In boundary fights the Tahsildar now uses the GPS-anchored LPM map, not the old paper sketch. Free instant view online; certified Tippon from the MRO takes 7–15 days and is what the registrar accepts at sale-deed registration. Sub-divided or merged in the resurvey? The old survey number alone will NOT pull the map — find the new LPM via your Passbook first. What Bhu Naksha is The visual half of the land record: the Passbook says who OWNS the land; the Bhu Naksha shows exactly WHERE it sits, what shape it has, which survey numbers touch its boundary, and how far it stretches on each side. Without the map, ownership paper never tells a parcel’s full story. Definition — Tippon / FMB copy: the certified measurement sketch of a single survey number issued by the Survey department — the offline, legal-weight counterpart of the online map view. Checking it online (free) 1) bhubharati.telangana.gov.in → GIS / “Cadastral Map” under Information Services — no login to view (the mobile app stays more stable than the desktop site during peak office hours). 2) District → Mandal → Village; the map zooms to the village with all survey numbers shaded. 3) “Search Survey Number” on the GIS toolbar — the parcel highlights; click it for the recorded extent in acres-guntas. 4) Print/download the PDF — and cross-check the same parcel on the ISRO Bhuvan Telangana viewer for an independent satellite overlay. Getting the certified Tippon (offline) MRO or MeeSeva → FMB Copy / Tippon application (issued by the Survey department under the 1923 Act) → form with survey number, village, mandal + Passbook or deed copy → the Mandal Surveyor processes after Tahsildar approval. Fees vary by service (one district lists ₹295 for sub-division applications, ₹1,410 for demarcation appeals). 7–15 days; the copy carries the surveyor’s seal and signature — the version the registrar accepts at registration. Tip: apply for the village map and Tippon TOGETHER; combined requests cost less. Reading the map, field by field Field What it means What to check Survey number / sub-division Legal parcel identifier Match exactly to the seller’s passbook entry LPM number GPS-anchored resurvey ID Confirm PERMANENT, not Temporary Extent Area in acres-guntas Compare with passbook — post-drone, ground reality wins Boundary lines Shape + adjoining survey numbers Walk all four sides; check encroachment Land classification Wet, Dry, Shikam, government Reject Shikam / government shading without clearance Village / mandal / district Administrative location All three must match the deed Good sign: closed boundary, Permanent LPM, extent matching the passbook, no overlap with neighbours or government colour shading. The six map problems, and fixes Survey number returns blank — sub-divided/merged in the drone survey or record in a holding state: search by Passbook number for the new LPM, then ask the Tahsildar for record reconciliation. Online extent ≠ passbook — the GIS survey applies a “ground reality rule” (drones measured 1.95 acres where paper said 2.00 → record becomes 1.95): file RoR Correction before the 13 April 2026 deadline if the gap is unfair. Parcel overlaps government/assigned land — the map can reveal slivers over Shikam, Waqf, forest or 22-A-flagged land: pull the village’s Prohibited Lands list; if the survey number appears, walk away. Seller shows an old printed Tippon — fraud rings have used outdated sketches to sell government land as private: refuse any map older than the April 2025 cutover; demand a fresh live download in your presence. Map vs ground mismatch — fences and walls drift over years: use Know Your Position — stand on each corner with GPS on. Two parcels show overlap — a record conflict; resolve at the MRO before any deal. Example: The “fresh map or no meeting” rule: any boundary conversation runs on a map downloaded TODAY, on someone’s phone, in everyone’s presence. Old printouts are how government land gets sold as private. Quick answers (FAQ) Bhu Naksha vs Tippon? Online view vs certified offline sketch of the same map. Cost? Viewing free; Tippon fees vary — confirm at the MRO. Why did my survey number stop working? Resurvey re-mapping — use the LPM. Validity? Indefinite; auto-updates each survey cycle. Bottom line Paper says who owns; the map says WHAT exists. After the drone resurvey, the GPS-anchored map is the boundary truth Telangana’s own officers use — check it before every deal, and never against an old printout. For you: For a plotting developer the Bhu Naksha is the FIRST feasibility tool: shape, road-touch, neighbours and government shading — visible before a single site visit. Overlay it with your Land Scout map layers, and make the fresh-download-in-presence rule non-negotiable on both sides of your deals. tg-bb-bhudhaar: Key Highlights The Bhudhaar is Telangana’s unique parcel ID, generated against GPS-mapped boundaries — two parcels cannot share one, which is what makes double registration hard. It exists in TEMPORARY and PERMANENT states — and the registration slot opens only against a verified permanent Bhudhaar. It travels with the PARCEL, not the owner: sales change the pattadar; the Bhudhaar persists. It must print identically on the record, the passbook, the certified copy and the (new) sale deed. Sources describe its digit count differently — treat the number on YOUR record as authoritative and quote it exactly. What it is, and is not Its job is disambiguation: survey numbers repeat across villages, subdivisions blur, paper descriptions drift — the Bhudhaar cuts through by binding ONE number to ONE mapped polygon of ground. Parcels enter the system with a temporary ID; verification of boundaries and records upgrades it to permanent — and everything downstream (the slot, increasingly lender scrutiny) keys on the permanent state. It is the parcel’s Aadhaar in spirit: identity for land, persistent across owners. Definition — Temporary vs permanent Bhudhaar: temporary = the parcel is in the system but its boundary/record verification is incomplete; permanent = verified. Registration refuses temporary or absent IDs — which is why the status check comes before any money. Finding yours (two minutes) 1) Land Details Search on bhubharati.telangana.gov.in with survey number or LPM — the Bhudhaar prints on the record itself. 2) Read the STATUS: permanent or temporary. 3) Cross-check the Pattadar Passbook carries the SAME number as the live record — a mismatch needs resolving before any deal. 4) Download the signed certified PDF — it embeds the Bhudhaar for anyone verifying later; lenders and buyers will ask for exactly this. Where it appears — all must agree Location Role If it disagrees Pahani / RoR 1B The live record’s identifier The record is the reference point Pattadar Passbook Owner’s document Update the passbook via the MRO Certified copy PDF Embedded with the QR Re-download; verify the QR resolves Sale deed (new) Binds deed to parcel Correct BEFORE execution, not after Slot booking Precondition check Slot refuses temporary or absent IDs Good sign: a permanent Bhudhaar printing identically on record, passbook and certified copy, quoted exactly in the draft deed. The four problems, and fixes Stuck at temporary — verification incomplete: pursue it via the MRO; the slot will refuse until permanent. Record shows no Bhudhaar — a migration gap (often with missing LPM linkage): raise at the Tahsildar with passbook and old records. Passbook and record differ — one predates a correction: align the passbook to the live record at the MRO. Deed quotes it wrong — a transcription slip that unravels the parcel linkage: fix the DRAFT; post-registration cures are painful. Why buyers check it first The cheapest fraud filter in Telangana: a parcel whose ID is absent, temporary or mismatched CANNOT complete registration — so every rupee advanced before the check is a rupee at risk. Make it step zero: confirm permanent status, confirm the number matches across record and passbook, screenshot the status for your file (so it shows when you checked), and only then spend money on deeper diligence. Example: The seller hurrying you toward an advance while the Bhudhaar sits temporary — “it will sort itself out” — is asking you to fund THEIR verification problem. Verified first, money second. Quick answers (FAQ) Why does registration need it? The agricultural slot opens only against a verified permanent Bhudhaar. Where is mine? On the Pahani/1B and the Passbook; the certified PDF embeds it. Does it change on sale? No — it belongs to the parcel; only the pattadar name changes. Record and passbook differ? Resolve at the MRO before any transaction. Bottom line One number, one polygon, one status check — the thread that joins paper to ground. Permanent and matching everywhere, or the deal waits. For you: Add a “Bhudhaar line” to your parcel sheet: number + status + screenshot date. In assemblies, run it across ALL survey numbers on day one — a single temporary-status parcel in the middle of your layout is a registration bottleneck you want to discover before the design, not before the launch. tg-bb-lpm: Key Highlights The LPM (Land Parcel Map) number is the identifier from Telangana’s GIS drone resurvey — each record linked to an exact mapped boundary. Bhu Bharati is shifting from survey-number to LPM-keyed records, with the Bhudhaar as the unique ID riding on top. Old deeds, ECs and family memory speak survey numbers; the live record increasingly answers to the LPM FIRST. Subdivided family land: one old survey number fans out into SEVERAL LPMs — one per parcel, each with its own Bhudhaar. Normal. The #1 “my record disappeared” complaint is just a survey-number search on a parcel that now answers to its LPM. Why the LPM exists A century of subdivisions, merged holdings and hand-drawn village maps left survey numbers pointing at ambiguous ground. The resurvey replaced that ambiguity with polygons measured from the air and verified on foot. The transition is the tricky part: both identifiers remain meaningful — what matters is confirming they refer to the SAME parcel. Finding yours and mapping it back Have the passbook? Start there — the LPM prints on the Pattadar Passbook for resurveyed parcels and is the fastest search key on the new portal. Then: search the record by LPM, confirm extent and pattadar match expectations; the record displays the LEGACY survey linkage — note both together, because your deed and EC still speak the old number; and quote the pair (plus Bhudhaar) in every diligence note and draft. Searches failing? Try each identifier in turn (survey → LPM → Bhudhaar; migration gaps affect them unevenly); ask the MRO to look up the survey-to-LPM mapping from resurvey data; and a parcel with NO LPM linkage gets flagged at the Tahsildar before any transaction. Survey number vs LPM Aspect Survey number (legacy) LPM (resurvey) Source Historic village survey GIS drone resurvey Precision Descriptive, drift-prone Mapped polygon boundaries Where cited Old deeds, ECs, memory Live record, passbook, portal Subdivisions Fractions of one number Separate LPM per parcel Future role Legacy reference Primary search key Good sign: a record where LPM, legacy survey number and Bhudhaar display together and match the deed’s description. The four transition frictions, and fixes Survey number finds nothing — the parcel answers to its LPM now: search with the passbook’s LPM; the record is almost certainly there. No LPM anywhere — the resurvey linkage hasn’t landed: raise at the Tahsildar; do NOT transact on an unlinked parcel. One survey, many LPMs — subdivided land fanned out: identify YOURS by extent and boundary before proceeding. Deed and LPM extents differ — small drifts are normal resurvey reality; large gaps need survey clarification first. What a diligence file now carries The triple, verified as one parcel: legacy survey number from the deed + LPM from the record + Bhudhaar as the unique key. A file with only the old number is running on the previous system’s assumptions. On the ground, the LPM is what the GPS position tool and the cadastral view key on — it lets you stand on the land and confirm you are inside the right polygon. Example: Red flag: a seller whose paperwork speaks only old survey numbers and who cannot produce the LPM or Bhudhaar is selling something the new system cannot yet see. Resolve that before money moves. Quick answers (FAQ) Is the survey number obsolete? Not yet — deeds and ECs cite it; the record shows the linkage; the LPM is becoming primary. Why several LPMs for one survey number? Subdivision → separate parcels, each with its own ID. My search fails — is the record gone? Almost never: use the passbook’s LPM. LPM vs Bhudhaar? Map identifier vs unique transaction ID — together with the legacy number they form the parcel’s full identity. Bottom line Speak both languages: the deed’s survey number for history, the LPM for the live system, the Bhudhaar to bind them. One parcel, three names, one polygon. For you: Update your land-bank register NOW: add LPM and Bhudhaar columns beside every survey number you track, and resolve the blanks at the MRO this month — not during a deal. In the Scout sheets, an LPM-complete parcel is a faster-closing parcel; price your urgency accordingly. Original Deccan Ledger guide lesson; full source guide on 1acre.in (links above).
