tg-bb-kyp: Key Highlights Know Your Position overlays your phone’s GPS on the cadastral map — showing which survey number / LPM polygon you are standing inside, with surrounding boundaries. It collapses one specific deception: the mismatch between the land SHOWN and the land DOCUMENTED. Orientation, not adjudication: consumer GPS drifts metres (more under trees) — legal boundaries stay with survey records and licensed surveyors. Run the check at the parcel’s CENTRE, not its edges — mid-parcel readings defeat GPS drift. Free, five minutes, done before any money conversation. What it does A site-visit verification tool in the Bhu Bharati ecosystem: record, seller and your own feet cross-checked in one glance. When that becomes routine, the two-fields-over trick — showing a beautiful parcel while the deed describes the scrubby one behind it — simply stops working. Use it inside its limits: a reading near a boundary line is a question, not an answer. Using it on a site visit 1) Open the tool via the portal ON SITE with location allowed — LOAD IT BEFORE ARRIVING; rural signal varies. 2) Walk to the parcel’s middle — centre readings defeat drift; edges invite it. 3) Read the survey number / LPM under your position; SCREENSHOT with the location visible. 4) Match against record, passbook and draft deed identifiers — any mismatch stops the conversation until explained. What GPS can and cannot settle Question Can GPS settle it? What settles it properly Am I on the documented parcel? Yes, at parcel centre Reading + record match Is this boundary line exact? No Survey records; licensed surveyor Does shown land match the deed? Yes, as a first check Full identifier match in diligence Where does the neighbour’s land start? Indicatively only FMB sketch; demarcation survey Is the extent as claimed? Roughly at best Measurement survey Good sign: a centre-of-parcel reading matching the record’s survey number and LPM exactly, screenshotted, filed beside the documents. Field realities, and fixes Drift near boundaries — read from the centre; treat edge readings as inconclusive. No signal on site — load beforehand, or capture coordinates and verify after. Reading disagrees with the seller — the polygon on screen is not the documented parcel: STOP; this is precisely the fraud the tool exists to catch. Map feels misaligned — rare base-map anomalies: cross-check the FMB; raise persistent cases at the MRO. Why every site visit needs it It costs nothing, takes minutes, and closes the one gap no document can: whether the ground under discussion is the ground on paper. Keep the output with the file — a dated screenshot of the reading beside the record extract is a tidy, persuasive piece of a diligence trail. Example: Red flag: the seller who keeps the walk at the parcel’s edge, discourages the GPS check, or explains a mismatched reading with “map errors” is showing you land they do not intend to sell you. Quick answers (FAQ) Is it legally conclusive? No — indicative; boundaries come from survey records and demarcation surveys. Accuracy? A few metres, worse under cover — centre readings reliable, edges not. Without signal? Load in advance or verify captured coordinates later. Extent check? Only roughly — measurement surveys settle extent. Bottom line Five minutes at the parcel’s centre, one screenshot, one match against the record — and nobody can show you one parcel and sell you another. For you: Standing operating procedure for your team’s site visits: KYP screenshot from parcel centre + fresh Bhu Naksha download, both timestamped into the parcel folder before any negotiation. And use it defensively on YOUR ventures — walk buyers to their plot’s centre and let their own phone confirm the plot; trust built by the buyer’s own device outlasts any brochure. tg-auto-mutation: Key Highlights Auto-mutation: agricultural sale-deed registration at the SRO automatically triggers the Pahani/RoR update to the buyer’s name — no separate application, under the 2020 RoR Act, now Bhu Bharati Act 2025. Before Dharani, deed and revenue record lived in two offices with no link; integration fixed that — in principle. In practice sync delays, migration errors and mismatches have left THOUSANDS of Pahanis showing the old owner after registration. Seven days is the unofficial ceiling — beyond it, the deed-vs-Pahani gap is a documented risk, and the grievance portal is your lever. A Pahani still naming the old owner is an open door for that person to apply for mutation under succession claims. What auto-mutation is Under the Telangana Rights in Land and Pattadar Passbooks Act 2020 (carried into the Bhu Bharati Act 2025), completing agricultural sale-deed registration at the Sub-Registrar triggers the portal to update the Pahani to the new buyer — no separate Tahsildar application. In 2025 Bhu Bharati replaced Dharani as the primary agricultural portal (dharani.telangana.gov.in now redirects); the auto-mutation concept carries forward, but migrated records may have gaps — so if a recent registration is not updating, check bhubharati.telangana.gov.in before concluding it is merely delayed. Checking your mutation (under two minutes) 1) Land Details Search → district, mandal, village, survey number → the Pahani should show YOUR name as Khatadar; the previous owner’s name means auto-mutation has not processed. 2) “Track Application” with the registration document number or application ID — pending / in-process / completed; “in process” after seven working days means the trigger has stalled (old Dharani-era IDs remain searchable on Bhu Bharati). 3) Stuck? Citizen Services → Grievance Redressal / Correction of Land Records — file with document number, registration date, survey number, and the registered deed attached. 4) After processing, confirm the Pahani shows your name, Passbook number and survey details — and screenshot/download the updated record immediately as DATED proof. Then apply for the updated e-Passbook: a Passbook in the old owner’s name breaks every future transaction, including loans. The offline escalation (Tahsildar/MRO) If the grievance stalls: 1) go in person to the mandal’s Tahsildar/MRO with the ORIGINAL deed and a copy of the portal’s “in process” screen. 2) Request manual correction — under Bhu Bharati this is handled at Tahsildar level (no Collector approval), cutting the wait. 3) Submit deed, Aadhaar, Passbook number, survey details; take the acknowledgment receipt. 4) Get the ORDER NUMBER and track it under RoR Corrections / Grievance Status; physical follow-up every 10 days is reasonable. Suspect a competing claim by the previous owner? Say so explicitly and ask for the survey number to be put under observation — do not rely on the portal in contested cases. Confirming it completed — field by field Field What it means What to check Khatadar name Current recorded owner YOUR name exactly as on the deed Passbook number New owner’s linked PPB New e-Passbook generated; old PPB deactivated Survey number + extent The parcel and its area Extent matches the deed — errors cascade into loans Mode of acquisition How ownership arrived “Purchase” + the registered transaction date Mutation date When the change recorded Must POST-date registration; earlier = data error Transaction history Chain of ownership changes Ends with the previous owner selling to YOU; gaps = incomplete chain Good sign: your name as Khatadar, mutation date within 7 days of registration, mode = Purchase, extent matching the deed, new e-Passbook generated with Aadhaar linked. Why the 7-day window matters Every day the Pahani still names the seller is a day the seller (or their heirs) can file a competing mutation under succession or other grounds — the documented Dharani-era fraud. The system closed the two-office gap; the sync delays reopened a smaller one. Your job is to close it fast: check on day 3, escalate on day 8, and never file the purchase away as “done” until the record and Passbook both say your name. Example: Calendar discipline: registration Monday → portal check Thursday → if unchanged the following Monday, grievance filed with the deed attached → ten days later, Tahsildar in person. Buyers who treat mutation as an event, not a consequence, are the ones the fraud never finds. Quick answers (FAQ) Do I need to apply for mutation after buying farmland? Normally no — it auto-triggers; your job is VERIFYING it happened. How long should it take? Within ~7 days. Stuck longer? Grievance online, then Tahsildar manual correction. Does this cover non-agricultural property? No — urban mutation runs separately through the municipality. Bottom line Auto-mutation is a promise, not a guarantee. Verify at day 3, escalate at day 8, screenshot everything — and the system’s convenience becomes real instead of theoretical. For you: Build the 3-day check into your closing workflow for every acquisition — assistant task, not memory. And for your plot buyers: a one-page “after registration” card (check Pahani day 3, grievance path, e-Passbook application) turns the state’s weakest step into your venture’s best after-sales moment. tg-bb-mutation: Key Highlights Mutation = updating the Record of Rights after ownership changes. Under the RoR Act 2025: sales auto-mutate; inheritance, succession and court-decree cases are filed with and decided by the Tahsildar. The sale sequence is tight: registration against a verified Bhudhaar → transaction flows to the land-records module → Pahani reflects the buyer within DAYS. Auto-mutation only works when registration ran on the verified Bhudhaar — mismatched-identifier deals are exactly the ones whose Pahani never updates. The old climb to the Collector is gone — Tahsildar decides, which is why timelines shortened. Until the Pahani and passbook carry the new name, the previous holder can still borrow against or resell the land on paper. The two paths Purchase (auto): the sub-registrar slot only opens on a verified permanent Bhudhaar, which links the deed to the parcel — that linkage IS what makes the automation work. Register, note your document number (your tracking key), wait days not months, then pull the Pahani and check your name, extent and classification character by character; the new pattadar passbook follows the updated record — keep the old owner’s documents until yours arrive. Inheritance (manual): heirs file at the village’s Tahsildar with the death certificate, legal-heir certificate and passbook; the Tahsildar may verify with family members and local enquiry before passing orders; track by application number, then pull the updated Pahani and passbooks for EACH heir. Documents required Document Used for Notes Sale deed Sale mutation Auto path; keep the document number Death certificate Inheritance Mandatory for succession cases Legal-heir certificate Inheritance Family Member Certificate from MeeSeva Pattadar Passbook Both Old passbook surrendered; new one issued Aadhaar Both Identity and eKYC of the parties Court decree Decree cases Certified copy with proof of finality Good sign: a Pahani showing the new holder within days of registration, extent unchanged, and a passbook issued in the SAME spelling as the deed. When mutation stalls — four causes, four fixes Pahani not updated after sale — registration ran on a mismatched or temporary Bhudhaar: raise via application status, then the Tahsildar with your document number. Record still names the deceased — no succession filing was ever made: file the inheritance case with heir proof; the record will not fix itself. Extent shrinks after mutation — a data-entry slip in the carry-over: file RoR correction IMMEDIATELY; do not drift toward the 2026 deadline. Family dispute freezes the case — contested succession goes to enquiry: expect a hearing; a registered family settlement speeds resolution. Why it matters after registration Plenty of buyers stop at registration and discover years later that the Pahani still names the seller — who has since mortgaged the land. The deed protects you in COURT; the record protects you in the MARKET; you want both. Diarise it: registration day → Pahani check within two weeks → escalation if nothing moved. Ten minutes closes the loop on the entire purchase. Example: Red flag: any seller or agent calling mutation “a formality you can sort out later”. The window where record and deed disagree is exactly where the frauds live. Quick answers (FAQ) Is mutation automatic now? For registered sales against a verified Bhudhaar — yes, within days. How do heirs mutate? Tahsildar filing with death certificate + heir certificate + passbook. How long? Sales: days; inheritance: weeks; anything past a month deserves escalation. Does mutation prove ownership? No — ownership flows from the registered deed; mutation aligns the record with it. Cost? Modest statutory charges — treat large “facilitation fees” as a red flag. Bottom line Sale mutation is automation you VERIFY; inheritance mutation is a filing you MAKE. Neither is optional, because the un-mutated window belongs to the previous owner’s creditors and schemes. For you: In JD assemblies the inheritance path is your critical path: land in a late father’s name cannot even sign your agreement until heirs mutate. Ask “whose name is the Pahani in TODAY?” at the first meeting, and where it is a deceased elder, budget the Tahsildar timeline into your deal calendar — or watch your launch date slip a season. tg-heir-cert: Key Highlights Processed in Telangana as the Family Member Certificate (FMC): the Revenue Department’s official record of a deceased person’s surviving spouse, children, parents and dependents. It serves NON-litigious claims — pensions, insurance, PF, land mutation; a court-issued Succession Certificate (Indian Succession Act 1925) is the separate document for recovering financial assets. Hindu Class-I heirs (spouse, sons, daughters, mother) inherit equally; Class-II (siblings, grandparents) only if no Class-I exists. Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020): daughters hold coparcenary rights BY BIRTH, married or not — omitting them makes later sale deeds voidable. Jurisdiction follows the deceased’s LAST RESIDENCE, not where the property sits; wrong office = automatic rejection. The Telangana HC (Global Industries) is clear: the MRO certificate identifies family members — it cannot decide contested titles; disputes go to civil court. What the certificate is — and its court-issued cousin Two documents overlap and get confused. The MRO/Tahsildar Legal Heir Certificate (technically the FMC, under the GHMC Act 1955 and land-revenue rules) suits routine claims and the initial MUTATION of land under the Passbook Act. A Succession Certificate comes only from the Civil/District Court and is what banks and institutions demand for recovering financial assets. Both can apply to the same estate at the same time, depending on what is being claimed. The FMC names every heir under the personal law applicable to the deceased. Definition — Class-I heirs (Hindu Succession Act 1956): the first circle — spouse, sons, daughters and mother — who inherit EQUALLY and exclude everyone else. Siblings and grandparents (Class-II) enter only when no Class-I heir exists. Applying online (MeeSeva) 1) Register at meeseva.telangana.gov.in — the same account handles caste, residence and FMC services. 2) Services → Revenue Department → Family Membership Certificate — the form lists deceased details, applicant details, and a ROW FOR EVERY HEIR (name, relationship, age, gender). 3) Upload: death certificate, applicant’s Aadhaar, relationship proof (birth/marriage certificate), latest address proof, ration card if available, deceased’s Aadhaar — affidavits from ALL heirs declaring no objection speed verification. 4) Pay the MeeSeva charges; note the reference number. The Tahsildar, VRO and Mandal Revenue Inspector verify and conduct FIELD inquiries within 15–30 days — the download unlocks the moment the Tahsildar approves, so check status daily after day 15. Applying offline (MRO) 1) Go to the MRO of the deceased’s LAST RESIDENCE — jurisdiction is fixed by residence, not property location. 2) Fill the form on ₹2 stamp paper: deceased’s full name, date of death, last address, complete heir list; attach death certificate, all heirs’ IDs, address proof, ration card; photos of all major heirs are usually asked. 3) Take the stamped acknowledgment with reference number — the VRO will verify the heir list with NEIGHBOURS at the residence. 4) After the enquiry clears, the Tahsildar signs and issues — demand the seal-and-signature page in clear original colour; banks routinely reject faded photocopies. What it contains, field by field Field What it means What to check Deceased’s name + date of death Whose estate this is Matches the death certificate — no spelling variants Last permanent address Anchors jurisdiction Must fall under the signing Tahsildar’s mandal List of legal heirs Every spouse, child, dependent parent Married daughters LISTED — their omission is the top defect Relationship + age + gender Class determination; pension/guardian use No minor child omitted, even under a different guardian Issuing authority Tahsildar / MRO Seal of the mandal where the deceased last lived Date + reference number System identity Verify the certificate is LIVE on MeeSeva by its number Good sign: every Class-I heir including married daughters, the right mandal’s seal, and a reference number that verifies live on the portal. The classic defects, and fixes Married daughters left off — a century of habit, now legally fatal: sale deeds built on a defective FMC can be set aside on suit; before signing anything, demand inclusion of ALL daughters. Tahsildar rejects a Class-II application — officials cannot mechanically refuse siblings/grandparents; where no Class-I heirs exist they must inquire — file a written representation citing the High Court’s position and escalate. Contested estates / NRI heirs — the FMC route is for the undisputed; contested inheritance goes to a declaratory suit in civil court. Example: Buyer’s use of this lesson: when purchasing inherited land, read the FMC yourself and COUNT the daughters. Three sons signing while two married sisters exist somewhere is not a discount opportunity — it is a future partition suit with your plot in the middle. Quick answers (FAQ) FMC vs Succession Certificate? Revenue-office family list vs court authority over financial assets — different jobs, sometimes both needed. Timeline? 15–30 days with field verification. Can the MRO decide who owns the property? No — identification only; title disputes are civil-court business. Do all heirs need to consent to a sale? Yes — every heir the certificate names (and every one it wrongly omits) must sign. Bottom line The FMC is the gateway document of inherited land: get it complete (daughters included), from the right mandal, verified live — and treat any incomplete heir list as a countdown to litigation. For you: Standing rule for buying from families: FMC + your own daughter-count + every heir’s signature (or registered release deeds) before any agreement. The missing married daughter is the single most common time-bomb in Telangana land deals — and the cheapest one to defuse at paperwork stage. tg-bb-ror-correction: Key Highlights RoR correction fixes Dharani-era errors — misspelled names, wrong extents, missing survey/LPM linkages, misclassification — filed at the Tahsildar. The window is ONE YEAR from the Act’s commencement (14 April 2025), closing 13 APRIL 2026 — after which entries attain finality. Four correctable buckets: identity, quantity, location, character. Ownership DISPUTES are not corrections — those go to civil remedies; deceased-on-record is MUTATION, not correction. Authority sits with the Tahsildar (appeals to RDO and Collector); decisions are time-bound. Old official paper wins: pre-Dharani pahanis, deeds, passbooks, survey records. What the window covers The Act’s bargain is simple: one clean year to challenge and repair the migrated record, after which casual correction closes. Generous compared to the Dharani years — brutal if you sleep on it. Correctable errors fall in four buckets: identity (name spellings, father’s name), quantity (extent mismatches), location (missing or wrong survey/LPM linkages), character (wet shown as dry, agricultural shown otherwise). Every week of delay stacks your case behind thousands racing the same date — and a rejection near the deadline may leave no time to cure and refile. Filing at the Tahsildar Paper wins these cases — assemble proof FIRST. 1) Pull the current Pahani and 1B and mark exactly which entries are wrong; precision here shapes the whole case. 2) Assemble proof: old pahanis, the sale deed, passbook, Aadhaar, survey records — the older and more official, the stronger. 3) File with proof at the Tahsildar; keep the NUMBERED acknowledgment — your tracking key. 4) Attend if called, answer the enquiry, then pull the corrected record and check EVERY character — confirm the fix did not introduce a new error. Errors and their winning proof Error Winning proof Watch out Name misspelled Aadhaar, passbook, old Pahani The fix must match the DEED spelling too Extent wrong Sale deed, survey sketch, old records Neighbouring claims can surface Survey number missing Old Pahani, FMB, resurvey LPM data Often an LPM-linkage issue, not loss Wrong classification Old Pahani, revenue records Affects value and conversion rights Deceased still on record — That is MUTATION: file succession instead Good sign: an acknowledged filing well before the deadline, proof that PREDATES Dharani, and a corrected record verified character by character. Why corrections fail (process, not merit) Wrong case type — succession and ownership contests filed as “corrections” bounce: inheritance → mutation; disputes → civil remedies. Thin proof — an application that merely asserts the right spelling goes nowhere: attach old pahanis and deeds. Missed hearing — non-appearance lets the case lapse quietly: track the number, attend every date. The fix breaks something else — verify the fresh record immediately and refile within the window if needed. Why the deadline outranks everything After 13 April 2026 the record you have is PRESUMED the record that is right. Loans, sales and registrations will run against it; unwinding an error shifts from a Tahsildar form to an uphill appeal with a heavier burden. For sellers an uncorrected record kills deals at scrutiny; for buyers it kills the loan. If you hold Telangana land and have not pulled the record since migration — do it this week. The check is free; discovering the error after finality is not. Example: Red flag: anyone advising you to leave a known record error “for after the deal” or after the deadline is trading YOUR legal position for THEIR convenience. File first, transact second. Quick answers (FAQ) Deadline? 13 April 2026. Who decides? Tahsildar; appeals to RDO/Collector. What can be corrected? Names, extents, survey/LPM linkages, classification. After the deadline? Finality clause — appeals only, slower and costlier. Sell with a pending correction? Technically possible, practically painful — mismatches stall registration and loans. Bottom line One free record-pull this week versus an appeal ladder next year: audit every parcel you own or plan to buy against the deadline, and let the calendar — not the counter clerk — drive the urgency. For you: URGENT for the land bank: pull the Pahani/1B for EVERY survey number you or your landowner partners hold, THIS MONTH, and file corrections on anything off by a letter or a gunta. Post-deadline errors become pricing discounts on your own inventory. Also screen acquisition targets: a parcel needing correction after finality is a longer, cheaper deal — negotiate accordingly. tg-ec: Key Highlights The EC lists every REGISTERED transaction on a property — sales, mortgages, gifts, leases, partitions, attachments — from the Sub-Registrar’s records. Form 15 = transactions exist (each with parties, numbers, deed type); Form 16 = Nil EC — and a Nil on ancestral land may just mean the family never registered anything. IGRS digital records start January 1983; earlier history lives in the SRO’s physical Index Books. Agricultural land: Bhu Bharati holds the recent records (2018+) — check BOTH portals for converted parcels. An MRO-level charge in the Pahani’s liabilities column may never appear in any EC — read the two together. Certified fees: ₹200 up to 30 years, ₹500 beyond; manual SRO searches take 15–30 days. What the EC is — and its two blind spots The Registration department’s statement of every registered transaction over a chosen period: reading the chain top to bottom shows how the land travelled to the present seller and what still sits charged on it. Blind spot one: TIME — digital records begin 1 Jan 1983; a seller who bought in the 1970s and held quietly has a clean online EC that says nothing about the early years; manual Index-Book search at the SRO is the only complete record for older parcels. Blind spot two: REGISTRATION — unregistered hand loans, pending litigation, unregistered agreements and MRO-level charges never appear; that is why the EC is read ALONGSIDE the Pahani, never instead of it. Getting it online 1) The right portal: urban/non-agricultural → registration.telangana.gov.in (Citizen login); agricultural → bhubharati.telangana.gov.in under Land Details Search; recently converted parcels → BOTH. 2) Online Services → Encumbrance Search (EC) → accept the disclaimer → search by document number (most precise) or property details (district, SRO, village, survey number). 3) Set the period: 30 YEARS for a purchase — short windows miss disputes that settled years ago but still shape the chain. 4) Form 15 or Form 16 appears; the free view is fine for research; for a bank file pay ₹200/₹500 and download the signed PDF IMMEDIATELY — the system does not always allow re-downloads without re-paying. Reading the entries Field What it means What to check Document number + year Each registered transaction’s ID Cross-check against the seller’s stated history; unexplained entries need explanations Deed type Sale, mortgage, gift, partition, release, lease An ACTIVE mortgage = debt on the parcel — cleared before your clean title Parties Names in each transaction Every name must connect to the next transaction — a non-connecting name is a break in title Consideration Declared value Oddly low old values sometimes hide real consideration — check context SRO details Where each deed registered Must match the property’s jurisdiction; cross-SRO deals on one parcel are a red flag Status Form 15 vs Form 16 Form 16 on old/ancestral parcels may be a FALSE negative — combine with manual checks Good sign: Form 15 with a clean chain ending at the current seller, no live mortgage, every transaction closing the previous one, one consistent SRO. The traps that cost real money Nil EC on quietly-inherited land — no registrations ≠ no claims: pair with the Pahani, possession enquiry and heir checks. The loan that never shows — deposit-of-deeds and MRO-recorded charges bypass the register: demand a bank no-dues letter and read the Pahani liabilities column. Chain breaks — a gap between transfers means an unregistered link document: trace it before proceeding; lenders will refuse the gap anyway. Pre-1983 assumed clean — never buy an older parcel on the online EC alone. Example: The 30-year discipline in one line: a 5-year EC can look spotless while a 12-year-old mortgage sits alive just outside the window. The default search period is set for convenience, not for your protection — always override it. Quick answers (FAQ) What period should I search? 30 years for any purchase. Is Form 16 good news? Only with corroboration. Is the online EC valid for banks? Yes — the signed digital certificate is accepted; banks re-verify the chain themselves. EC or Pahani? Both — registered charges vs possession/classification/revenue-level liabilities. Bottom line The EC answers one question with authority — what was REGISTERED — and stays silent on everything else. Thirty years, both portals for converted land, the Pahani beside it, and manual books for the pre-1983 years: that is a complete encumbrance check. For you: Your standard EC order for any parcel: 30-year certified pull by YOU (never the seller’s copy), same-day Pahani liabilities read, and for pre-1983 chains the manual SRO search budgeted into the deal timeline. On your ventures, include the 30-year Form 15 in each buyer’s file — it pre-empts the bank’s slowest query. Original Deccan Ledger guide lesson; full source guide on 1acre.in (links above). tg-igrs-ec: Key Highlights In Telangana the EC issues through IGRS at registration.telangana.gov.in — NOT through the Bhu Bharati land-records module; searching the wrong portal is the #1 confusion on the new system. Every registered sale, mortgage, gift, release and lien appears as an entry — parties, date, document number. The EC reflects registered documents ONLY: unregistered hand loans, pending litigation and unregistered agreements never appear. A 5-year EC can look clean while a 12-year-old mortgage sits outside the window — pull 30 years for purchases. Banks sanction against the EC chain, not the seller’s word: no release entry, no sanction. Where it lives, and why that matters Two systems, two jobs: Bhu Bharati holds the land RECORD (Pahani, mutation, Bhudhaar); IGRS holds the REGISTRATION side (EC, market value, deed copies). If you are hunting the EC inside Bhu Bharati you are on the wrong portal. Reading an EC chain top to bottom shows how the land travelled to the present seller — and what still sits charged on it. Pulling it, step by step 1) registration.telangana.gov.in → Encumbrance Search. 2) Pick the search key: document number + year if you have a prior deed (most precise); otherwise survey number or house number. 3) Set the period — 30 years for a purchase decision, never the default few. 4) Pay the statutory fee, download, SAVE the PDF — lenders will ask for exactly this. Entry-type literacy Entry What it is What it means for you Sale deed Ownership transfer Builds the chain to the present seller Mortgage Loan charged on the land Must be RELEASED before or at your purchase Release / discharge Loan closed Confirms an earlier mortgage cleared Gift / settlement Family transfer Check stamping and acceptance were proper Agreement of sale (regd.) A prior committed sale A LIVE agreement can block your purchase Lien / attachment Court or department charge STOP until formally lifted Good sign: a continuous chain old owner → present seller, every mortgage matched by a later release, no live agreement or attachment. The four casual-reader traps Nil treated as clean — nil means no registered entries IN THE WINDOW: widen to 30 years and still verify Pahani and possession. The missing loan — unregistered borrowings never appear: bank no-dues letter + Pahani liabilities column. Wrong property searched — survey-number typos and door-number confusion pull a different parcel’s EC: cross-check the EC’s schedule against the deed and LPM. Break in the chain — a gap suggests an unregistered link document: trace it first; lenders refuse gaps anyway. Why lenders read it first Sanction runs on the chain: mortgage without release = stop. Reading the EC the same way BEFORE your advance puts you ahead of the problem instead of behind it. Pair it always with the Pahani — EC for registered charges, Pahani for possession and classification; the two together are the minimum diligence for any Telangana purchase. Example: Red flag: a seller offering an EC for a conveniently short period, or discouraging the 30-year search, is steering you around an old entry. Pull the full period yourself — it is your ₹200, and your protection. Quick answers (FAQ) Where do I get the EC? IGRS — registration.telangana.gov.in, Encumbrance Search. Search without a document number? Yes — survey or house number; document-number is sharper. Valid for banks? Yes — the digital certificate is accepted; banks re-verify. EC or Pahani — which matters more? Both, together, always. Bottom line Right portal (IGRS), right key (document number), right period (30 years), right reading (every mortgage needs its release) — the EC is only as protective as the search you configure. For you: Teach your whole team the two-portal split — record on Bhu Bharati, registration on IGRS — because half of “the portal shows nothing” panics are wrong-portal searches. And keep a one-line entry glossary (this lesson’s table) pinned in your office: entry-type literacy is what separates reading an EC from merely downloading one. tg-22a: Key Highlights Section 22A of the Registration Act lets the state BAR parcels from registration entirely — once listed, the Sub-Registrar must refuse any sale, gift or mortgage deed. No discretion, no workaround. Six categories: government land, Endowment/Waqf, ceiling surplus, assigned land, court-disputed parcels, and land notified as against public policy. The 2017-18 records updation and the 2020 Dharani rollout WRONGLY flagged thousands of genuine private patta parcels; an Aug 2025 high-level committee is reviewing a list covering over ONE CRORE acres. The list updates continuously and not in real time on every device — check the DAY you decide, and again the morning of registration. The Telangana HC requires inclusions to follow Rules 238–241 (2016 Registration Rules) and to cite the specific clause — improper listings are challengeable. What 22A is The state’s registration firewall: survey numbers on the prohibited list simply cannot register. It protects public assets in theory; in practice the list’s errors create TWO buyer risks — the obvious one (you try to register, the SRO blocks, your money is stuck) and the subtle one (the parcel looked clean on an old check, and the 22A flag surfaces at the counter because the portal was not refreshed). Definition — The clause ladder: 22A-1(a) assigned land · (b) government land · (c) Endowment/Waqf · (d) ceiling surplus · (e) court-ordered restriction · (f) government-notified prohibition. Each carries different weight — (a) cannot be sold without government regularisation; (e) can dissolve when the case does. Knowing WHICH clause tells you whether resolution is even possible. Running the check (free, two minutes) 1) Agricultural : bhubharati.telangana.gov.in → Land Details Search → district, mandal, village, survey number → read the “Prohibited Status” column. 2) Urban/non-agricultural : registration.telangana.gov.in → “Prohibited Properties” → same details; a red indicator or a clause like “Under 22A-1(a)” means blocked at the SRO. 3) Read the SPECIFIC clause, not just the status — it decides whether there is any path forward. 4) SCREENSHOT with the date visible — if the status changes between your check and registration day, you hold documented proof of what it showed when you decided. Always check BOTH portals THE SAME DAY: survey numbers clean on one have appeared prohibited on the other in known cases. What the result shows Field What it means What to check Survey number The parcel checked Exactly matches the parcel shown on the GROUND Prohibited status Blocked from registration or not Any flag = SRO refusal; no exceptions without a delisting order 22A clause Which sub-clause applies Decides removability — (a) needs regularisation; (e) tracks the court case Reason description Why it is listed Cross-check the seller’s explanation; inconsistency is a serious warning District / mandal / village Location of the entry Match the physical location, not just the seller’s paperwork The offline route, and fighting a wrong listing At the SRO or Tahsildar: ask for the prohibited-register entry for your survey number — under HC guidelines it must show the DATE of inclusion and the clause; an office that cannot produce them may be sitting on a procedurally challengeable listing. Genuine patta land wrongly listed: file a grievance through Bhu Bharati’s TM 15 module (inclusion-in-prohibited-list grievances) with title deeds and Passbook attached — the Collector is the competent authority for removal under most clauses; if Revenue fails to act within 90 days, the High Court can be approached for a writ of mandamus. The timing trap Properties have been ADDED to the list between a buyer’s first check and registration day — blocking the transaction after money had moved. The discipline: check on the day you finalise the price, and again the morning you go to the SRO. Dates matter; screenshots prove them. Example: For perspective: with over one crore acres on a list under active review, the 22A check is not paranoia about rare fraud — it is hygiene on a system the government itself admits needs auditing. Two minutes, two portals, one dated screenshot. Quick answers (FAQ) Can 22A land ever be bought? Only after formal delisting — clause-dependent; assigned land effectively never. My genuine patta land is listed — what now? TM 15 grievance with proof → Collector → writ after 90 days of inaction. Which portal? Both, same day: Bhu Bharati for agricultural, IGRS for urban. Is a clean check permanent? No — recheck at every decision point. Bottom line One list decides whether your deed can even be presented. Check both portals on decision day, read the clause, screenshot the date — and treat every listed parcel as unbuyable until a delisting order says otherwise. For you: You already run 22A as gate one — upgrade it to the full protocol: BOTH portals, same-day, clause noted, dated screenshot into the parcel folder, and a re-check the morning of every registration in your ventures. For wrongly-listed landowner partners, knowing the TM 15 → Collector → writ ladder makes you the developer who can actually unlock their stuck parcel — a sourcing edge nobody else in the room has. tg-bb-prohibited: Key Highlights Section 22A lets the state notify land whose sale documents the sub-registrar MUST refuse — maintained as a searchable list of survey numbers on IGRS. Categories: government, assigned, endowment, wakf and court-attached land — each fails a purchase for a DIFFERENT reason. Prohibited parcels look normal on the ground and often carry plausible-looking paper — the LIST, not the seller’s file, is the authority. PARTIAL listings exist: one subdivision prohibited, the rest free — so the check runs on the exact survey number and extent. A 22A listing is not a complication to manage — it is a BAR. Stop until the entry is formally deleted. Why each category fails differently Government land was never the seller’s to sell. Assigned land was granted to the landless with restrictions that persist for decades. Endowment and wakf property belongs to institutions whose alienation needs statutory sanction, rarely granted. Attached land is frozen by a court until told otherwise. The buyer’s trap is uniform though: on the ground they all look like ordinary parcels with ordinary fences. Running the check on IGRS Free, no login — the single highest-value two minutes in Telangana diligence. 1) registration.telangana.gov.in → prohibited property search (a REGISTRATION-department list). 2) Drill to district, mandal, village — and confirm the REVENUE village; boundaries shifted in places. 3) Search the exact survey number AND its subdivisions where they exist — partial prohibitions attach to subdivisions. 4) If listed, note the CATEGORY — it decides the (rare) cure path. Categories and cure paths Category Why it is barred Any path forward? Government land Not the seller’s to alienate None for a private buyer Assigned land Granted with transfer restrictions Only per the assignment law’s own terms Endowment property Institutional land; sanction needed Statutory permission — rare in practice Wakf property Wakf Board alienation rules Board sanction — exceptional Court attached Frozen pending proceedings Only after the attachment lifts Wrongly listed Clerical / legacy entry Deletion via RDO / Collector with proof Good sign: a clean search on the exact survey number and its subdivisions, saved as a dated screenshot beside your EC and Pahani. The four complications, none of which excuse skipping it Wrongly listed parcel — legacy and clerical entries occur: the OWNER applies for deletion via RDO/Collector with ownership proof; you buy only after formal removal. Partial listing — a subdivision is barred, the rest free: get the exact extent and subdivision mapped by survey records first. “Deletion is imminent” — promises substitute for nothing: wait until the entry actually vanishes, and recheck yourself. Assigned land offered cheap — the classic void deal: restrictions survive the sale and the money rarely comes back. Walk. Why 22A precedes the EC An EC tells you about charges on a SALEABLE parcel; the 22A list tells you whether the parcel is saleable AT ALL. Run it first — no clean EC rescues a prohibited survey number. And recheck near registration: lists update, and the gap between first search and SRO appointment is exactly where surprises land. Example: Red flag: a seller pushing urgency on a bargain-priced parcel while discouraging a free two-minute list check is telling you, indirectly, what the check would say. Believe them. Quick answers (FAQ) Does a clean EC override a listing? Never — the EC reports charges; 22A bars registration entirely. Can assigned land be bought? Only within the assignment law’s narrow terms. Wrongly listed? Owner pursues deletion; you wait for the record, not the promise. Recheck before registration? Always — dated screenshots of both checks. Bottom line Order of operations is the lesson: 22A first (is it saleable?), EC second (is it clean?), everything else after. Exact survey number, subdivisions included, dated screenshot, recheck at the SRO date. For you: Pair this with the deep-dive assigned-land and 22A-check classes in the school — together they are your acquisition firewall. Process upgrade: your parcel folder’s first page should be the two dated 22A screenshots (decision day + registration morning). When a lender or JV partner audits your venture, that page answers their first question before they ask it. Original Deccan Ledger guide lesson; full source guide on 1acre.in (links above). tg-bb-slot: Key Highlights Slot booking is the appointment system for executing registration — agricultural land books inside Bhu Bharati and REQUIRES the parcel’s verified permanent Bhudhaar; non-agricultural books through IGRS. The Bhudhaar precondition is the anti-fraud spine: no verified parcel identity, no slot — which blocks the old double-registration scripts. Stamp duty is paid by challan BEFORE the appointment, on the higher of government value and deal price; the challan number joins the booking. Parties, not just papers, must attend: executants, claimants, witnesses, with ID — a missing party is the top reason a confirmed slot produces no registration. Book only after the document set is COMPLETE — slots taken on hope become reschedules. How the system works The slot ties the deed to a uniquely identified parcel before anyone sits at the registrar’s desk. Practical consequences: your booking problems are usually IDENTIFIER problems in disguise (a temporary Bhudhaar, a mismatched record); and the money must be sequenced correctly — duty computed on the higher-of rule, paid by challan, amounts matching, before the appointment exists. Booking, step by step 1) Confirm the Bhudhaar: verified PERMANENT status on the record — temporary means fix that first; everything else waits. 2) Compute and pay the challan on the higher of government value and deal price; keep the challan number with the deed draft. 3) Book: office, date, time; enter parties, parcel and challan details — choosing a slot ALL parties can actually attend. 4) Attend with the full set at the booked hour — late arrival can forfeit the slot on busy days. What to carry Item Who needs it Notes Sale deed (final) All parties Printed per drafting rules; unsigned until told Challan proof Buyer typically Amount must match the duty computation Aadhaar / ID Every party and witness Names matching the DEED spelling Pattadar Passbook Seller Links the parcel to the record Photographs Parties Per current office requirements PAN where applicable Parties High-value transactions require it Good sign: a slot booked after EC, 22A and Bhudhaar all cleared, a challan matching the duty maths, every party present with ID at the hour. The four failure patterns Slot will not open — temporary/unverified Bhudhaar: resolve on the record; the slot follows. Challan mismatch — paid duty ≠ computed base: recompute on higher-of and regularise before the date. A party cannot attend — one missing executant voids the appointment: reschedule EARLY per portal rules, don’t forfeit on the day. Documents fail scrutiny — name mismatches, stale EC: correct the record, pull fresh checks, rebook clean. The exam-day framing Everything earlier converges here: Pahani, EC, 22A, market value, Bhudhaar all get CONSUMED at this appointment. Buyers who did the sequence sail through; buyers who skipped steps discover it at the registrar’s desk with money already committed. Treat the appointment as the exam and the checks as the syllabus — nothing new should be learned at the SRO, because anything learned there is learned with your money on the table. Example: Red flag: an agent promising a same-day slot on a parcel whose Bhudhaar is still temporary is promising to bypass the one control that protects you. Whatever the method — decline it. Quick answers (FAQ) Why does the slot need a Bhudhaar? So the deed binds to a uniquely identified parcel — the anti-double-registration control. Where do I book? Agricultural: Bhu Bharati; non-agricultural: IGRS. When is duty paid? Before the appointment, by challan, higher-of rule. Can I reschedule? Yes, within portal rules — early beats forfeiting. What kills appointments? Missing parties, challan mismatches, unverified Bhudhaar, record-name discrepancies — every one checkable the week before. Bottom line The slot is a gate that only opens on completed homework. Book late in your process, not early in your optimism. tg-bb-market-value: Key Highlights The government “market value” (basic value) is the per-unit rate for each survey number/locality, maintained by the registration department on IGRS. Duty and fees compute on it — or on the deal price if HIGHER. Under-declaring saves nothing: duty still charges on the government value, plus scrutiny. Units differ: agricultural per ACRE, non-agricultural per SQUARE YARD — and adjacent survey numbers can carry sharply different rates (highway-touch vs behind it). It lives on IGRS, not Bhu Bharati — the most common dead-end search on the new system. Pull the rate EARLY: duty and fees are a meaningful percentage, and lenders expect you to know the number. What the value is The state’s floor price for stamp-duty purposes, survey number by survey number. The higher-of rule is what buyers miss: declare below the government value and duty is still charged on the government value; declare above and duty follows your price. There is no arbitrage in under-declaration — only legal exposure. (This is Telangana’s version of the guideline-value concept covered in the school’s tax classes.) Checking it (free, two minutes) 1) registration.telangana.gov.in → Market Value Search — the registration department’s service. 2) Choose the LAND TYPE first: agricultural (per acre) vs non-agricultural (per square yard) — pick wrong and the number misleads you. 3) District → mandal → village → survey number; adjacent surveys can differ sharply. 4) Note the unit rate, multiply by your extent, keep the figure for duty maths — and compare against your negotiated price; the higher prevails. Where the value bites Stage How it applies What to do Budgeting Duty + fees computed on it Add them to the deal price early Negotiation A large gap either way needs explaining Ask WHY the price sits far from the rate Registration SRO applies higher-of Carry your computation; verify the challan Bank loan Valuers cross-check both figures Expect questions on big divergence Resale later Capital-gains reference values Keep the rate record from purchase day Good sign: a deal price sitting explainably near the government rate, duty computed on the correct base, a challan matching your own maths. The four value-check mistakes Wrong land type selected — agricultural rates read against a non-agricultural parcel or vice versa: re-run with the classification from the Pahani. Deal far below the rate — duty charges on the government value anyway and the gap invites scrutiny: price honestly. Adjacent-survey confusion — the neighbour’s premium rate read as yours: confirm exact survey number and LPM before computing. Rate seems outdated — revisions land periodically and portals lag: verify at the SRO for a live transaction; carry a dated printout. The negotiation read Sellers quote prices; the state quotes values — and the DISTANCE between them is information. A price far above the rate needs justifying features (frontage, corner, road width); far below it needs an explanation that is not a title problem in disguise. Do the full arithmetic before your offer — price + duty + fees — because that total, not the sticker, is what competes with other parcels. Example: Red flag: anyone proposing to register below the government value “to save you duty” is proposing something that does not work arithmetically and exposes you legally. Decline. Quick answers (FAQ) Where do I check? IGRS Market Value Search — not Bhu Bharati. Duty on price or value? Whichever is higher. Same rates for farm and urban land? No — per acre vs per square yard; the search asks first. Why is the next survey different? Rates set survey by survey — roads, use and locality lines create sharp steps. Does it affect my loan? Valuers compare both figures; unexplained divergence slows sanction. Bottom line Know the state’s number before you argue about the seller’s. Right land type, exact survey number, dated printout, higher-of maths — and the challan will never surprise you. For you: Track basic-value REVISIONS across your belts like market intelligence — the state raising a village’s rate is the state telling you where it sees demand (and your buyers’ closing costs rising). And in negotiations, open with the IGRS rate printed: anchoring on the state’s number moves family sellers more than any comparable you quote. tg-bb-status: Key Highlights Application status is the portal’s live view of any filed request — mutation, correction, certificates — tracked by acknowledgment number. The number is not a receipt; it is the case’s IDENTITY. Quote it and any office finds the file; lose it and you are asking strangers to search thousands of filings by name. The arc: submitted → under verification → enquiry/hearing → approved/rejected → record updated. Verification is where thin-document files sit. Time-bound processing under the RoR Act means stages carry expectations — six weeks parked at verification is NOT normal anymore. Correction cases race the 13 April 2026 deadline: track weekly; a late-discovered rejection may leave no room to cure and refile. Tracking online 1) bhubharati.telangana.gov.in → application tracking (mutation, correction and certificate requests). 2) Acknowledgment number + captcha → current stage and HOLDING OFFICE — and save a screenshot each time; the screenshots build your timeline. 3) Read the stage honestly: submitted and verification are normal early; weeks without movement are not — note the office named, because that is where you follow up. 4) Act on outcomes: approved → pull the updated record and VERIFY it; rejected → get the reason and cure fast — near deadlines, refiling is a same-week task. Escalating offline Start at the Tahsildar: quote the number, ask what the file awaits, supply it that day if you can. Persistent non-movement goes up one level to the RDO — WITH your dated screenshots. Revenue grievance days and MeeSeva complaints create the written record of delay that escalation runs on. The stage ladder Status What it means Your move Submitted Filed, not yet picked up Wait; recheck in a week Under verification Officer examining documents Ask what is missing if it lingers Enquiry / hearing Field check or appearance needed ATTEND — absence lapses cases Approved Orders passed Pull the updated record and verify Rejected Refused with a reason Cure the defect; refile fast Record updated Change reflected in Pahani Download a fresh certified copy Good sign: a file moving stage to stage within days, a named office you can visit, an outcome verified against the fresh record. The four tracking failures Number returns nothing — typo, or the filing never entered the system: recheck digits, then confirm at the filing office with your paper acknowledgment. Stuck at verification for weeks — thin documents or a parked file: visit the Tahsildar with the number; supply what is missing in person. Rejected without a clear reason — demand the specific defect IN WRITING; you cannot cure what is unnamed. Approved but record unchanged — sync lag: allow days, then raise the mismatch with the ORDER number at the MRO. Why watching wins A weekly check with dated screenshots turns you from a hopeful petitioner into a DOCUMENTED one — and documentation is what the RDO responds to at escalation. For buyers mid-transaction the tracker is protection: never release the final payment while the seller’s promised correction or mutation still reads “submitted”. And usefully — WITH the number, the portal shows anyone the status: buyers can verify a seller’s claimed filings before paying. That is deliberate. Example: Red flag: an agent who says “the application is moving” but cannot produce the acknowledgment number is describing an application that may not exist. No number, no filing. Quick answers (FAQ) What number do I need? The acknowledgment number from filing. How long per stage? Days to a few weeks; past a month deserves escalation. Rejected — now what? Specific reason → cure → refile, same week near deadlines. Can I track someone else’s application? With the number, yes — use it to verify sellers’ claims. Bottom line The acknowledgment number is the case; the weekly screenshot is the strategy; and payment against a promise waits until the tracker says the promise came true. For you: Two standing rules for your operation: an “applications register” (number, filed date, stage, next check) reviewed every Monday for everything pending across your parcels — and in purchase agreements, milestone payments tied to TRACKER STATES (“on mutation showing approved”), not to seller assurances. The portal becomes your escrow officer. Original Deccan Ledger guide lesson; full source guide on 1acre.in (links above). tg-can-i-buy: Key Highlights Telangana has NO state-origin restriction and NO farmer-status requirement: any Indian citizen can buy agricultural or non-agricultural land in all 33 districts. All categories accessible: agricultural, horticultural, residential, commercial, industrial. Ceiling caps (Ceiling on Holdings Act 1973) still apply per family — wet 10–27 acres, dry 35–54 (up to ~65 in drought-prone zones). Section 22-A blocks registration of government, ceiling-surplus, waqf and assigned land statewide — with 1+ crore flagged acres under committee review (GO Ms 98, Aug 2025), statuses CHANGE: re-verify just before registration. Buying in another person’s name to dodge restrictions is BENAMI: 1–7 years rigorous imprisonment, fine to 25% of fair value, confiscation. Who can buy The clean answer: everyone Indian. Unlike states that restrict farmland to agriculturists, Telangana runs open — no domicile test, no farming background, every district from Hyderabad and Rangareddy to Warangal and the fringe belts. The Bhu Bharati Act 2025 modernised the records behind that openness, assigning each parcel an 11-digit Bhudhaar ID that makes outsider transactions cleaner. The ceiling caps Open does not mean unlimited. Under the Ceiling on Holdings Act 1973, a FAMILY (of five = one standard holding) may hold: irrigated (wet) land 10–27 acres depending on soil class A–D; dry land 35–54 acres by soil class E–K, stretching to ~65 acres in drought-prone zones. Holdings AGGREGATE across all districts toward one ceiling. Violations bring registration refusal — and excess land is seized as ceiling surplus. Definition — Standard holding: the ceiling unit for a five-member family; larger families scale within limits. The cap counts everything the family holds statewide — scattering purchases across districts does not reset it. Where 22-A cuts across All 33 districts are open — but Section 22-A blocks registration of government-owned, ceiling-surplus, waqf and assigned land statewide. The moving part: GO Ms No. 98 (August 2025) created a committee to rationalise MORE THAN ONE CRORE flagged acres, so a parcel’s status can change on the portal — verify before negotiation AND re-verify just before registration. The due-diligence checklist ☐ 22-A prohibited list + waqf status on Bhu Bharati BEFORE any negotiation. ☐ Title search — 12-year minimum via Bhu Bharati (agricultural) or IGRS (non-agricultural); 30 years for high-value purchases. ☐ Tahsildar clearance that the family’s AGGREGATE holding stays within ceiling limits. ☐ Converting agricultural to non-agricultural? DTCP/HMDA/revenue approval + NALA tax before registration. ☐ Stamp and register at the SRO — budget 4–5% duty, with biometric verification mandatory from January 2026. The benami line — read it twice Buying land in ANOTHER PERSON’S name to circumvent restrictions — origin, residency, occupation or tribal-area rules — is a benami arrangement under the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act 1988 (as amended 2016). Penalty: 1–7 years rigorous imprisonment PLUS a fine up to 25% of fair market value; the property can be CONFISCATED and the deed cancelled. Power-of-attorney workarounds, ownership-mimicking 99-year leases and shell-company structures are not recognised — do not attempt them. Example: The framing that keeps people honest: in Telangana there is almost never a reason to structure creatively, because the front door is open. Anyone proposing a name-lending or PoA structure for a purchase you could lawfully make directly is importing risk you do not need. Quick answers (FAQ) Do I need to be a farmer? No. Can NRIs buy? Non-agricultural yes; agricultural land is barred by FEMA regardless of the state’s openness (see the NRI class). How much can a family hold? Ceiling-dependent: 10–27 wet / 35–54 dry acres. The one check that cannot be skipped? 22-A — twice: at decision, and just before registration. Bottom line Telangana’s door is open; the discipline is inside the house — ceilings, the 22-A list, honest names on deeds, and a record system that now enforces all three. For you: This is your one-lesson answer for every out-of-state or first-time investor who asks “can I even buy there?” — send them here. For your own assemblies, watch the CEILING maths on landowner families: a family already near its cap cannot take your developed-plot consideration as land without breaching it — structure JD returns accordingly. tg-hmda-dtcp: Key Highlights HMDA layout approval sanctions layouts within the Hyderabad Metropolitan Region; DTCP covers everywhere else (Telangana Urban Area Development Act 1975). Both assign the LP number that gives a layout legal standing. A Gram Panchayat sanction is NOT layout approval — it carries no weight for registration or bank loans; buyers who confused the two have paid for plots they cannot register. Since April 2024, new HMDA applications run on BuildNow (buildnow.telangana.gov.in); DPMS handles older files and CLU; DTCP districts use dpms.dtcp.telangana.gov.in. The RIGHT portal matters: a valid LP number searched on the wrong portal returns nothing — creating false alarm or false confidence. HMDA holds developer plots as MORTGAGE security during approval — some are not released for sale; check whether yours is one. Which authority, which portal HMDA territory: Hyderabad, Medchal, parts of Rangareddy, Sangareddy, Medak, Siddipet, Bhuvanagiri. DTCP: every other district. A seller waving HMDA approval for a plot in Nalgonda, Karimnagar or Khammam has raised the first red flag — those are DTCP territory. Portals: pre-April-2024 HMDA layouts → dpms.hmda.gov.in; post-April-2024 → buildnow.telangana.gov.in; DTCP → dpms.dtcp.telangana.gov.in. Converted zones near Hyderabad that moved between jurisdictions during boundary changes can have entries on BOTH systems — check both. Verifying the LP number Free and instant. 1) Ask the seller for the approval PROCEEDINGS order and the LP number with year — before any other conversation. 2) Search: DPMS public search by file number/applicant/project (filter by district, mandal, dates); BuildNow’s application tracking; DTCP portal by district + LP number. 3) Read status AND the attached conditions; download the approved layout DRAWING — exact plot boundaries, road widths, open spaces as sanctioned — and match it against the physical site. 4) The LP number must appear on the proceedings document AND the drawing, matching the portal exactly; a developer who cannot produce them, stop. What the approval contains Field What it means What to check LP number The layout’s legal identity On proceedings + drawing + portal, all matching Approved drawing Sanctioned plan: plots, roads, open spaces Site must MATCH it — discrepancies mean plots sold outside the plan Approval authority HMDA or DTCP by location Authority must match the district Developer + survey numbers Applicant and parcels covered Cross-check deed survey numbers fall INSIDE the approved extent Conditions Roads, open-space handover, drainage Unfulfilled conditions = approved but not legally complete for sales Open Space Reservation Areas that cannot be sold or built Verify YOUR plot number is not in the reserved zone The offline route — and the mortgage check HMDA main office: Swarna Jayanti Complex, Ameerpet (visiting hours 3–5 pm); DTCP at AC Guards or district offices. Ask for the complete layout PROCEEDINGS for the LP number — the physical order with conditions, open-space requirements and road dedications, more detailed than the status screen — and the stamped approved drawing, matching your plot number against it. Then the check most buyers never run: is your specific plot one HMDA holds as mortgage security? HMDA takes developer plots as security during approval; some are not released for sale until the mortgage is discharged. The office confirms release status — and the DPMS public search shows mortgaged plots for many layouts. Run it before ANY advance. Example: The trap in one sentence: a genuine LP number does not make YOUR plot saleable — it can sit in the OSR zone, outside the approved extent, or under HMDA mortgage, all inside a “fully approved” layout. Verify the layout, then verify the PLOT. Quick answers (FAQ) Is panchayat approval enough? Never — no weight for registration or loans. Which portal for my district? HMDA belt → BuildNow/DPMS; everywhere else → DTCP’s DPMS. What if the number returns nothing? First confirm you are on the RIGHT portal; then treat as unapproved until proven otherwise. What makes a layout “complete”? LP number + conditions fulfilled + your plot inside the drawing and outside OSR/mortgage. Bottom line Three verifications, in order: the AUTHORITY matches the district, the LP NUMBER matches portal-proceedings-drawing, and YOUR PLOT sits clean inside the sanctioned plan — released, saleable, outside the reserved areas. For you: Your ventures live under these regimes — so weaponise transparency: print the LP number, portal link and approved drawing into every brochure, and walk buyers through the mortgage-release status of their specific plot unprompted. In a market where “approved layout” is the most abused phrase, showing the machinery is the premium. Original Deccan Ledger guide lesson; full source guide on 1acre.in (links above). tg-hmda-dp: Key Highlights HMDA Development Permission is the formal sanction for layouts, group housing, multiplexes and high-rises in the metropolitan region — under the HMDA Act 2008 and TS-bPASS Act 2020. Two stages: TENTATIVE layout plan (after AI scrutiny of drawings + fee), then FINAL LP after officials physically inspect roads, drainage, parks and parking on the ground. Every approved layout carries a unique LP number (format LP No. 000123/HMDA/LO/YYYY) — the single anchor a buyer must check. HMDA layouts must MORTGAGE 15% of plotted area with the municipality — released only after amenities are physically built and certified. From late 2025 every fresh application files through BuildNow; TG-bPASS stopped accepting new submissions 15 Dec 2025. Older approvals stay valid; only the filing route changed. What the permission is The only document that turns raw land inside the metropolitan region into a legally developable, marketable layout. HMDA’s writ runs across seven planning zones — including Ghatkesar, Medchal, Shamshabad and Shankarpally — with the Metropolitan Commissioner signing off on the Director’s recommendation. The two-stage structure is the buyer’s friend: a TENTATIVE LP means drawings passed scrutiny; only the FINAL LP means the roads and parks physically exist as sanctioned. Definition — Tentative vs Final LP: tentative = the plan is approved on paper; final = the District Level Committee / HMDA inspected the ground and certified it matches the drawing. Plots sell safely against FINAL status — a venture marketing hard on a tentative LP is selling a promise, not a layout. The application flow (developer’s view — and the buyer’s map of it) 1) Register on BuildNow — separate logins for owner and the Licensed Technical Person (only HMDA-listed architects, engineers, surveyors can submit drawings); the registration name must match the sale deed EXACTLY or the file bounces at scrutiny. 2) The LTP uploads architectural and structural drawings, layout plan, soil report, rainwater-harvesting plan, EC, tax receipt, 30-year link documents and self-certification declarations — the AI engine validates against zoning, road widths and FAR in minutes. 3) The Director approves / returns / rejects; on approval the Commissioner signs and a FEE LETTER lands — development charges, scrutiny fee, betterment charges, 1% labour cess — payable within 15 days. 4) The digitally signed Proceedings and Drawings auto-issue, LP number on every page — then run that number through dpms.hmda.gov.in public search to confirm it is live. Offline still handles: mortgage deeds, infrastructure-completion proofs, the physical site inspection that moves tentative → final, and the mortgage RELEASE order (office at Swarna Jayanti Complex, Ameerpet, 3–5 pm). Reading a DP, field by field Field What it means What to check LP number The layout’s permit ID Loads on the DPMS public search — instantly File number Internal application reference Cross-check on Online DPMS Survey numbers + village Parcels covered EVERY deed survey number inside the LP — one number off means uncovered Plotted area + open space Sellable extent + reserved 7.5% parks + 1% social infrastructure Your plot inside the plottable zone, not on reserved land Mortgaged plots The 15% held as security REJECT any mortgaged-list plot unless a release order is produced Road widths + setbacks Internal roads min 12 m, master-plan frontages Walk the layout — narrow roads and missing footpaths signal incomplete development Land use + zone Master Plan 2031 designation Not in a Conservation Zone, FTL or lake/tank buffer Sanction date + validity Issue date and conditions Old LPs without infrastructure compliance can be REVOKED — ask for current status Good sign: a digitally signed proceedings PDF with HMDA seal, an LP number that loads instantly, every survey number matching the deed, the mortgage list clearly marked. The frauds this system catches Fake LP numbers on impressive PDFs — the number simply does not exist on the public search: stop the deal; run BOTH the LP and file numbers through DPMS in your own presence. Phase-mixing — a genuine Phase 1 LP waved over Phase 2 plots the sanction never covered: match YOUR plot’s survey number to the approved extent, not the brochure’s. The mortgage blind spot — plots inside the 15% security sold before release: the DPMS search and the Ameerpet office both confirm release status; check before any advance. Example: The FTL/buffer line in the table deserves its own sentence: Hyderabad’s costliest demolitions have been buildings inside lake buffers with paperwork that looked fine. The master-plan layer check is not a formality in this city — it is THE check. Quick answers (FAQ) DP vs layout approval? The DP is the broader sanction family (layouts, group housing, high-rises); the layout LP is its plotted-development face. Which portal now? BuildNow for everything fresh; DPMS for legacy checks. What releases the 15%? Physically built amenities + District Level BuildNow Committee certification. Can old LPs die? Yes — non-compliant ones can be revoked; always ask for current status. Bottom line One number anchors everything — but the professional read goes three layers deeper: tentative or final, your survey numbers inside the extent, your plot outside the mortgage and the buffers. That is the difference between buying a plot and buying a proceedings PDF. For you: This is your own compliance playbook as you step into HMDA-belt development: budget the 15% mortgage into project cashflows from day one (it is trapped inventory until amenities finish — which is ALSO why finishing roads early pays twice), keep the deed-name-vs-BuildNow-registration identical, and hand buyers the DPMS search result for their exact plot. tg-building-plan: Key Highlights The sanctioned plan is the urban local body’s permit that your design follows the master plan and the Telangana Municipalities Act 2019 — without it the building is illegal from day one. It covers everything on the plot: setbacks, floors, height, parking, water/sewage, boundary walls — issued as a stamped drawing + proceedings letter. From 15 Dec 2025, GHMC, HMDA and DTCP applications ALL route through BuildNow, with AI scrutiny checking drawings against zoning in minutes. Plots up to 75 sq yards building G or G+1 need NO plan sanction — just online registration (₹1 token) and the fee with the first tax receipt. If 21 days pass with no action, DEEMED APPROVAL kicks in under the TS-bPASS Act 2020. The stick: every district’s Collector heads a Special Task Force that demolishes unauthorised buildings WITHOUT prior notice (s.174(4), TMA 2019). What the sanctioned plan is The permit for everything you intend to put on the plot. Legacy TG-bPASS sanctions on older buildings remain valid; every fresh application after the December 2025 cutover sits on BuildNow. The system’s design bargain: fast, AI-checked, self-certified approvals — matched by demolition powers that need no notice. Build inside the plan and the state is quick; build outside it and the state is quicker. Applying online 1) Register on BuildNow — citizens, owners, builders and Licensed Technical Persons each get separate registrations; token ₹1. 2) Your LTP submits drawings, structural details, sale deed, link documents, EC, latest tax receipt and the layout’s LP number; the AI validates against the Building Rules in real time. 3) On a technically clean file, the fee letter arrives by SMS/email — scrutiny fees, development charges (G.O. 223), 1% labour cess, user charges — payable in 15 days. 4) Proceedings, sanctioned drawing and BP order land as PDFs; if 21 days pass without action, deemed approval applies. Keep a digital AND hard copy on site — inspectors ask. Applying offline (panchayat areas) Outside GHMC/HMDA/DTCP zones: the mandal or municipality office → application form + fee schedule → filled form, deed copy, tax receipt, layout approval, engineer-signed drawings, challan → the town-planning officer inspects (setbacks, road width, clearance from heritage, water bodies, high-tension lines) → Building Committee sanction → stamped plan + BP proceedings. Cross-check the file number on the notice board or the DTCP site to confirm authenticity. The four problems buyers inherit Built area exceeds the plan — the extra slab, the closed-in setback: even ~10% deviation invites penalty; have an engineer measure against the sanctioned drawing before buying, and demand any regularisation order. Plan doesn’t match the site — a real-looking stamp mapped to a DIFFERENT plot or older proposal: punch the BP number into Citizen Search; survey number and address must mirror the ground. Restricted-zone plots — Conservation Zones, tower-line and water-body buffers: pull the master-plan layer; a restricted shading means no genuine sanction exists. Sanction obtained by misrepresentation — revocable under the Act, and then the task force arrives; verify deed dates against the G.O. 251/261/265 cutoffs where relevant. Example: For flat and villa buyers the lesson compresses to one motion: BP number into BuildNow Citizen Search, on your own phone, before the token advance. The seller’s PDF is a claim; the portal is the fact. Quick answers (FAQ) Do small plots need sanction? Up to 75 sq yd, G/G+1: registration only. What is deemed approval? 21 days of authority silence = approved, by law. Is a TG-bPASS sanction still valid? Yes — legacy sanctions stand; new filings go to BuildNow. Who demolishes? The Collector-led Special Task Force — without prior notice. Bottom line Telangana made legal building fast precisely so illegal building has no excuse. Verify the BP number yourself, measure the setbacks yourself — and never buy a deviation, however charming the extra floor. For you: As you move from plots into construction, BuildNow discipline IS brand discipline: sanction before slab, zero deviation, plan displayed on site. And in acquisitions, price every deviated building as if the deviation must be regularised or removed — because under this Act, one inspection can make that literal overnight.
